utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we begin, let me say at the outset that Judge May being indisposed, Judge Kwon and myself are sitting pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Mr. Theunens, you remain subject to the declaration that you made. And Mr. Tapuskovic, last day that we met, ten minutes was set for your cross-examination. You may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours and Mr. President Robinson. In the course of these ten minutes, I'm sure you will recall that we broached this subject, I was asking the expert witness something about a document I showed him, so might we have the document shown to the expert witness once again. I wanted to put certain paragraphs to him which I wasn't able to do because our time was up. So just a few documents of a document exhibited in September 2002, which comprises 300 pages. I would just like to put several paragraphs to the witness and ask him some questions about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, you know that on the 1st of July, 1991, Stipe Mesic, under the influence of the European Community, became president of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or, rather, the President of the Presidency of the SFRY. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I replied last time to this question, related questions, this is outside the scope of my report. However, I do recall that there were certain problems already on the 15th of May when Stipe Mesic was supposed to become the president of the SFRY but he didn't obtain the required majority, and the EC, or currently the EU, became involved in trying to find a peaceful solution. I also recall the negotiations that took place in Brioni on the 7th and 8th of July. But to answer the question, I didn't analyse that aspect of the conflict in detail for my report as it is outside the scope of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Theunens, your report or, rather, the summary of your report, reads as follows: "The armed forces of the SFRY and the conflict in Croatia." That's the heading, a title. And precisely because of that I'd like to present certain paragraphs from that report or, rather, from the document, and it is the Presidency session of the 12th of July, the first and only Presidency session held within that composition under the Presidency of Stipe Mesic which dealt exclusively with questions of what the armed forces of the SFRY should do, should undertake. The Chief of the General Staff, Kadijevic, and even Ante Markovic was present, the Prime Minister of the federal government. And the only person missing was Drnovsek. And if you look at page 1 of that document, do you agree with that, with what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, would you take a look at the English version of page 36, the sixth and seventh paragraphs on that page. In paragraph 6 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreters apologise, they don't have a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- Kadijevic is speaking, and would you pay attention to the several sentences before, and you will see that it is Kadijevic speaking about the place and role of the army and the goals of the army, the objectives of the army of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And that is in paragraph 6; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't know how many pages the document counts, but these are apparently minutes and I believe Mr. Tapuskovic when he says it's Kadijevic who is speaking, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I've just read out. He says the following, in paragraph 7 now, speaking with the tasks of the army, its essence lies in the following: "First and foremost to have all armed conflicts cease throughout the territory of the SFRY within the space of four days, to demobilise all armed formations on the territory of the SFRY except the JNA." So isn't it right that that's what he asked the Presidency to do, that a decision be taken for that objective to be fulfilled? Is that what it says here in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on this paragraph indeed. In this paragraph, Colonel General Kadijevic or army General Kadijevic, sorry, indeed requests, makes that request on the 12th of July. Now, I think it's obvious from other sources, like for example the book of Kadijevic and the orders I discussed in the reports, orders from the SSNO as well as the Chief of General Staff of the JNA that the situation--

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please excuse me, but I don't have time to go into all that. I've just presented a document to you, and you spoke about Kadijevic's book yourself. Take a look at page 85 of the English version, please, paragraphs 1 and 2 of that page. The majority were in favour of Kadijevic's proposal, the one that we've just set out. And in the previous paragraph he asks for just four days, a four-day deadline to have the paramilitaries disarmed, the units that were operational throughout Yugoslavia, and the majority agreed. And this is what Bogicevic says - he was the president of the Bosnia-Herzegovina - on page 85, you have it, and it is before you. "When it comes to the first proposal to cease all armed conflicts throughout the territory of the SFRY, I absolutely agree with that, and I think that the establishment of peace is the sole guarantee for us to move towards negotiations. Whether we'll succeed, and I'd like us to succeed within the space of 24 hours not even with us in the space of four days." So that was -- those were the views presented by the majority, and is that what it says, or words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is what the paragraph says, but again, it's a --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I would still like to say, I mean, it's a very long document, and I find it dangerous to draw conclusions based on certain paragraphs without having had the opportunity to look at the other paragraphs. Of course I can read too, I know what this paragraph says, but I'm not in a position to say whether this paragraph reflects the contents of the whole document because it is just a paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We note what you have said. Continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you spoke about Kadijevic's book, and I know that you respected what he said in the book, but I don't think you remember that the document that was produced on the first day of the Croatia trial, which is 300 pages long and it exclusively focuses on the work of the army of the SFRY and its efforts to disarm the paramilitaries, that you failed to organise this document. So it is my duty to quote several paragraphs to you and put them to you to ask you why the army wasn't given the green light to go ahead and disarm the paramilitary. So how is it possible that you have not had occasion to see this document and analyse it and you've been working in the OTP for so many years? Why didn't you look at the problems linked to the conflict in Croatia? Could you give me an explanation for that, please.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the three parts of the document, or the report, I believe there are around 400 documents footnoted. I think it's also clear from the -- what is described in the beginning of the report in the scope as well as executive summary that my task was mainly a military analysis task. My task was not to analyse the sessions of the SFRY Presidency or to act as if I were a legal analyst. My understanding of the various sessions of the SFR Presidency and the various meetings is that indeed there were a lot of discussions about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. arming, disarming, taking measures and so on, but I didn't judge it necessary or didn't consider it necessary to go into details into that matter as it --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to ask Mr. Theunens to clarify two more matters with respect to this report, and I'd like to ask for his comments, and my final question would come after presenting two more paragraphs to him from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On page 194 -- or rather, the English version is 171, page 171, paragraph 5, this is -- above that it says Kadijevic addresses everybody there and says the following, as far as point number 1 is concerned, it is so crucial that, as you were able to see, the new variant to withdraw from Slovenia, he didn't sidestep that point because the future of Yugoslavia ultimately is either a civil -- a civil war and it will depend on point 1 regardless of what will happen in Slovenia. Ante Markovic's response to that was, "I completely agree." And Kadijevic then says this is the key point, the crucial issue, and whether there will be a war or not depends on that key point. Is that what it says, or words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will repeat my previous answer to similar questions. This is one paragraph out of a quite long document, 252 pages. I can read the paragraph. I agree with what Mr. Tapuskovic has read as far as this paragraph is concerned. I'm not in a position to compare it with other paragraphs of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now take a look at page 228, paragraph 2. Stipe Mesic says when everything was over and when everybody was in favour of taking the decisions, Stipe Mesic said, and this is what it says here: "Very well, you can take that decision, make any decision you like, but I cannot sign the -- a capitulation here and that you are seizing Croatian territory." And at one paragraph further on, he says: "I can't go back to Croatia tomorrow as a traitor. That's out of the question. You can arrest me, you can do what you like. Do you want me to tender my resignation? If you do, I will do so." Is that what it says? And Mesic as president of the Yugoslav state Presidency did not want to stand behind the positions taken by all the other Presidency members to give a deadline of four days to the army to disarm the paramilitaries. To disarm the paramilitaries. I said the army but I meant paramilitaries, yes. And in that connection, Mr. Theunens, my final question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. TAPUSKOVIC [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In a situation of that kind, if the Yugoslav People's Army had the monopoly of violence, was the sole person which had the monopoly of violence, and if they were asking, the Presidency was asking to disarm the paramilitaries to prevent any further conflicts all over Yugoslavia, was that something that was of significance for further developments in Croatia, since the very next month all the barracks were blocked in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I find it very difficult to make comments more or less out of the loop or out of the blue on one paragraph of a quite extensive document which discusses a very complicated matter, a complicated, complex matter which is actually not completely within my field of expertise as I focused on the military aspects of that conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is your last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more point, please, with the Court's indulgence. And here's why, and this is why I'm asking this last question of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens says that this does not come within his remit to say anything, and in paragraph 8 it says: "The task of the armed forces of the SFRY was --" and this is from his summary -- "to pretext the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of the country and the social order as provided for by the SFRY constitution." Now, how, then, was it possible for the -- how could the army of the SFRY fulfil its duty and obligation if the decision that the army wanted the Presidency to take could not be implemented? How could it fulfil its role if what you say in the summary in paragraph 8 is correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 of the executive summary is the executive summary, so it's based on, as far as the mission is concerned, that mission is indicated and defined in the 1974 constitution and is of course confirmed in 1992 Law on All People's Defence as well as relevant JNA regulations, so I'm not in a position to discuss whether this is -- this is correct or not correct; I just read these legal documents and I quoted from there. And the second part of paragraph 8, where the evolution of the actual implementation of that mission is discussed, that's based on my review of JNA orders, SSNO orders, statements in the SSNO bulletin signed by Kadijevic and/or General Adzic, and last but not least, Kadijevic's book. If my task had been to analyse --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... not to continue. Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. Mr. Nice, last day you had indicated that you would not re-examine. Is that still your stance?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was prepared to waive re-examination on the last occasion in the interests of brevity, and I'm not going to change my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: However, can we deal with exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've -- in order to save time, I've filed a short motion making a proposal as to how exhibits might be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have -- we have the motion in hand, and I am to say that the Chamber accedes to the motion except for the third paragraph of the relief sought, that is, that the balance of the documents be marked for identification so that the other exhibits can be marked as proposed, and Judge Kwon will oversee the marking with the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Grateful. And then there's also tab 22 to be added, which is a document. I don't know whether Mr. Theunens knows if it's being added or not but if he's got it there then I ask him just to have a quick look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The proposed additional exhibit, tab 22, just explain what that is, please, Mr. Theunens, if you're immediately familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a report prepared by the 2nd Military District where the commander, General Milutin Kukanjac, makes an assessment of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina as it is during the March time period in 1992. I reviewed this document before, and it was also used in the third part of the report, the section -- the part that deals with the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know whether you want me to go further into details.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, that's fine. And, Your Honour, for those following the evidence and with an eye to the detail of how evidence is being dealt with, the proposal made to the Chamber in the short motion that I filed is that the 20 or more binders of material that Mr. Theunens has examined and that are reflected in his and Mr. Borrelli's reports remain available, as it were, through the conclusions in the report but aren't otherwise to be produced and to burden the court record save for the 22 tabs in the exhibit. We propose to the Chamber alternative ways of dealing with it and are entirely intent, of course, with the outcome, the position being that if at a later stage of the trial it is necessary to look at one of those documents in detail, you will have to take the appropriate step at that stage to look at the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. As for tab 22, which is just being introduced, the accused should have a chance of looking at it. The Chamber is disposed to -- Mr. Milosevic, have you had a chance to look at tab 22 which was just given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have not, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We will give the accused a chance to look at that, and we'll come back to that specific tab later. Mr. Theunens, that concludes your evidence, and you may go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As there is no witness in the courtroom just now, I should like to take this opportunity to ask you two things, to raise two matters. I have received a schedule for our sessions, the 4th of February, and I'd just like to quote two paragraphs, and I'd like an explanation about that from you, please. You say the following: "Considering that the accused must prepare [In English] for five longer sitting days in circumstances where he is currently unwell and because the longer sitting days will create a requirement for the accused to make preparations outside of the normal sitting schedule, it is appropriate for the Registrar to provide whatever reasonable assistance the accused may require to prepare for court." [Interpretation] The next paragraph says: "Noting that Judge May, due to illness, will not be available to sit in the trial when the trial recommences on the 10th of -- 2004 --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Just a minute, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The order speaks for itself. The Chamber was of the view that since you're ill, it would be appropriate for the Registrar to render whatever assistance he could to you, and I expect that he's doing that. The Chamber is of the view that it is important that this -- the Prosecution case be completed within the next two weeks. That is as much as we'll discuss in relation to that matter. Mr. Nice, next --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just tell you something, Mr. May -- Mr. Robinson and Mr. Kwon. I don't see what the Registrar could do. That's the first point. And secondly, the Registrar has done nothing. And then I have a further question, Mr. Robinson. A moment ago I received the prolongation of the ban on communication, that is to say for the third month running. And as you know full well, once you finish your half time that that false accusation has over there, then it's my turn to function. So how do you assume that I will be able to function even under conditions where I -- there is a ban on my communicating with anybody?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is a matter which the Chamber will look at in due course, I can assure you. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before the witness is brought in, Mr. Nice, the -- you will, of course, have received the order that the Chamber made in relation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've received the order, and we've made preparations accordingly. The witness, as you know, made an extensive statement from his own notes, and in order to deal with matters swiftly, I'd ask that he be allowed to have that with him as an aide-memoire and I can take him to paragraphs and I can deal with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The statement is very long, and we were concerned that the examination-in-chief and indeed the cross-examination should be focused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It will be. But if he could have the document as an aide-memoire, then it will make life much easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, he can have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I trust the Court and everybody else has the exhibit binders. I'm going to ask that all the exhibits be produced in due course, and I shall use the list of exhibits as another way to move through the evidence very swiftly. While we're waiting for the witness, if a provisional exhibit number could be given for the binder I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 645, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The legal officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Diego Enrique Arria.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A Venezuelan, holder of various high offices, permanent representative for Venezuela at the United Nations in 1992 and 1993, currently holding unpaid office at the United Nations as Assistant to the Secretary-General, and other posts well documented and available in detail if anybody wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon me, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear the question, I'm sorry? Venezuelan, permanent representative to the UN for Venezuela in 1992 to 1993, former governor of Caracas, holder of various other high offices and academic posts, and currently with an unpaid position at the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've publicly and in the course of a very long statement that's available but not produced here, expressed views that are highly critical of various parties and non-parties to the conflict, including the United Nations and the international community generally; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to focus on two aspects of evidence that you can help us with. They are these: First, I want you to summarise through exhibits and through your evidence the way and ways in which to your knowledge the accused and governments in Serbia and Yugoslavia were put on notice as to what was happening in the territory. Second, I want you to help us from your knowledge and experience of what effect that had on any sense of impunity that may have existed in those territories. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the first case, the Yugoslavia -- the former Yugoslavia, was for the people in the part of my world an extremely prestigious country and we were completely in support of preserving the integrity of Yugoslavia until the end of 1991. And when events start turning in the wrong direction, it was beginning of 1992, the end of 1991, is when we put it -- put a notice to the accused of the direction the events were taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to have to ask you to be responsive to questions because of the very great limitations of time. You have an index of exhibits and you also have the exhibits to your left-hand side. They can be -- the index can be laid on -- or a copy of the index can be laid on the overhead projector. We don't have time to go through it in detail. But were there several Security Council Resolutions about the former Yugoslavia and about Serbian involvement there of which, in general terms, you're critical on the grounds that they were either too strong or too weak, which was it?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: They were too weak. They were not relevant to really putting a stop to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in your judgement, what effect did that have on the people on the ground and on the Serb parties in particular?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It definitely created the impression that the international community was not about to put a red light. Was not precisely a green light but was not really meaning to do anything forceful to stop the developments on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tabs 1, 2, and 3 of what will be Exhibit 615 are some of those Resolutions. The Chamber has seen others of them through other witnesses. Can you turn, please, to tab 4, very briefly, which is a letter from Branko Kostic, vice-president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, denying all allegations made, this letter being the 30th of May of 1992 - a little out of order in the bundle, but never mind - and if we turn to the second page of that, we see setting out following denials of all allegations against the former Yugoslavia, firstly respect -- that it respects territorial integrity; secondly, that it will use all means to stop the fighting; third, it will prevent military organisation; fourth conditions be ensured to enable efficient and unhindered distribution of humanitarian aid; fifth, reaffirm strong opposition to forcible expulsion. Just yes or no: In your speech in the United Nations in due course on this topic, did you deal with those five assertions by the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was any one of them true?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn to the next exhibit in the file, tab 5, a letter from Mrs. Ogata, dated the 18th of March of 1993. This is a letter that has on page 1 an account of receiving verbal assurances from this accused and Dr. Karadzic on the 16th of March of that year, but on page 2 of the letter - this can be shown on the overhead projector if there's time but I can't delay so I will be dependent on the usher's good offices - on page 2 it says: "I also wish to draw your attention to the medium term developments in Srebrenica. I consider it absolutely necessary to maintain a permanent international presence in the enclave. This is the only means to ensure that the desperate population is not totally abandoned." And she's ready to maintain her own staff there. "Everything would indicate that a massive humanitarian tragedy is unfolding in the Srebrenica enclave. I believe that key world leaders should be alerted to these developments. I hope that what is happening today in Eastern Bosnia can be brought to the attention of the participants of the international conference." When did you first see that letter, Mr. Arria?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I saw this letter almost 11 years later, after it was never revealed or shared with the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You make many comments, we don't have time to expand on them, criticising the Security Council's failure to disseminate or even to have information available; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Go to tab 6, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let me just ask Dr. Arria: Whose underlining is it in the two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam Ogata's, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's her emphasis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's her emphasis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 6 is a letter from the then Secretary Boutros-Ghali of whom you are extremely critical generally, which has, as we see, general distribution. In short, would "general" have included distribution to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second page of tab 6 is the letter to which he refers. What he says, and we can see his description on the first sheet, is in line 3 -- he refers to a letter which is a second letter from Mrs. Ogata. It describes the disturbing situation which has developed in Srebrenica. Does that match the first letter or is that different in tone?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It complements the previous letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next letter we see, however -- no, I meant does Boutros-Ghali's observation reflect the tone of the first letter or --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Not at all. Madame Ogata actually, Your Honour, urged the Secretary-General to bring key leaders into the matter and with a great sense of urgency, and it took about 12 days for the Security Council to hear again about the situation while the people in Srebrenica were beginning -- were under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we see at the second two -- the second and third sheet of tab 6 the letter of the 2nd of April set out in an annex setting out the plight of the people in Srebrenica in paragraph 1, and over the page, as I must deal with this briefly, it can all be read at leisure, second paragraph: "Under these circumstances, I believe we are faced with two options if we are to save lives. The first is to immediately enhance international presence in order to turn the enclave into an area protected," and then she goes on to deal with other assistance that must be given. That letter, therefore, and what it reflected of the position on the ground, was available to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We then see at tab 7 a note by the president with general distribution of the Security Council. First paragraph: Shocked and alarmed at the dire and worsening position. Second paragraph, the Security Council recalls and affirms its relevant Resolutions and condemns the disregard and wilful flouting of the Bosnian Serb party which once again, in pursuit of its unlawful, unacceptable, and abhorrent policy of ethnic cleansing has blocked humanitarian relief efforts. And in the third paragraph, four lines up from the bottom, recalls on strict compliance with Security Council Resolutions. That letter was available?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 8, we see the first of two, I think, letters from Sacirbey. How were Sacirbey's complaints of what was happening treated?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: They were almost totally disregarded. It was a total sense of blase, another complaint by Sacirbey coming to the Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was Bosnia, in your judgement, taken as seriously as it ought to have been at that time in any complaints it made?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It was not. We live in a sort of a climate of denial of what the whole world knew was taking place, but not -- the Council was not very much interested in accepting the collective knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was this attitude connected, in your judgement, to any particular position taken by Council or, rather, UN members to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, definitely. We always felt, in aligned countries in the Security Council, that there was a great fear -- there was a double standard being applied in the case of Bosnia versus the standards that we applied in the case of Kuwait shortly before, and there was a fear of the emergence of a Muslim country in the middle of Europe and that they were being treated not as Europeans but as Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 9, please. A document we haven't looked at yet but which was available because of its being an order from the 8th of April from the International Court of Justice. This was an order on the complaint of Bosnia. We don't have time to look at the Bosnian complaint in any detail, but it's all set out, what they were complaining. But if we go to three or four pages from the end of the document, and we can see it at the top page 24, bottom of page 25. The court under a heading "Application of the Genocide Convention" ordered unanimously that the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia should immediately take measures within its power to prevent the commission of the crime of genocide, and then by 13 votes to 1, with the Russian I think not voting, that they should in particular ensure that any military, paramilitary, or irregular armed units which may be directed or supported by it, as well as any organisations and persons which may be subject to its control, direction, or influence do not commit any acts of genocide or conspiracy to commit genocide or direct and public incitement to commit genocide. So this was a publicly available order following a publicly available complaint.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You regard that as an important document, and did you at the time regard it as important?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Very important, significant document, Your Honours. So much so that we, the non-aligned countries in the Security Council struggled to actually have it recorded in a Resolution and to be acknowledged, coming from the International Court of Justice. There was great resistance to the inclusion of the Council of genocide at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And explain so that we can understand, on such a document, how long would normally or might take before some Resolution could be passed and some action could be taken? Could it be done the same day or the following --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It could have been within the next 48 hours, and especially coming from the International Court of Justice, which was the second time in my memory that I recall that addressed the Security Council. First it addressed in the case of Libya and second in this case it was done. It should have deserved urgent treatment by the Security Council, coming from the International Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in this case, as we see tab 11, you have to wait until the 15th of April, until your letter as coordinator transmits the copy of a statement. The statement we see on the following page. All of this is available for general distribution. The statement comes from the non-aligned countries; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in the middle of the first sheet, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The tab number should be ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did I not say 10? I apologise, tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The paragraph headed, "In this context we consider an extremely -- as extremely serious the postponement of the adoption of the aforementioned draft Resolution." This was your draft Resolution; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "The Bosnian Serb party has given ample proof that it is not willing to heed to any goodwill efforts to peace." Then you deal with Vance-Owen. Next paragraph towards the bottom of the page: "We stand behind the principles contained in the draft Resolution." Last paragraph you deal with the lifting of the arms embargo for which you pressed. And your view on the existence of the arms embargo was what? What effect did that have on Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: We consider that when the arms embargo was imposed on the countries in 1991, at the end of November 1991, we thought that this was a very significant, important measure, but we didn't know that actually we were preordaining the outcome of this conflict because the only side that was not armed, to have a regular armed forces, was actually the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and no one informed the Security Council or the permanent members of this situation. So it was innocently believing that this would put all the parties in similar condition. That was not the case at all, as time proved to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the draft Resolution itself is at tab 11 where, as drafted by your non-aligned group, you pressed for reaffirmation of position against ethnic cleansing. You reaffirmed the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and pressed for the establishment of this Tribunal. On the second sheet we see at number 3 concern at the refusal to accept the agreement of interim arrangements, demands observations of a cease-fire and full respect for rights of UN. This draft Resolution never got passed; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your judgement on what would have been the consequences of its being passed at that time had there been the will to do so?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It was very clear and evident that the Security Council was not going to go, Your Honour, beyond what it had already done, so we thought if they lifted the arms embargo would level the situation, and there was a complete agreement on the majority of the countries of the United Nations but not the Security Council where the Resolution was voted 9 to 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Returning to the issue of impunity that may or may not have been created, was the atmosphere and the attitude that was apparent to you in the United Nations something that should have been or would have been available to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. So much so I remember that the Yugoslavian ambassador at the time, Jokic, used to send letters, Your Honours, to his colleague in Venezuela, informing exactly what we were doing in the private consultations of the Security Council. I remember one day telling to Jokic that I wasn't going to send more reports to my own government about my performance in the Security Council because his reports were more fully informed than even mine, and presented even faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if it was coming to Venezuela from the Security Council, your inference is that it was going at the same speed and the same quality to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I have to imagine that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We then come to the mission, and the only mission, I think, of the United Nations to Srebrenica at the relevant time; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You pressed for that mission and led it.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the way, tab 12 is another letter from Sacirbey, you would say characteristically not taken seriously?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The same situation, even though at the time all these letters were corroborated by the international media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And also tab 14 as well. If we please in your -- you using your statement as an aide-memoire because the Court has allowed you to do so, go to page 40, and it's -- I'm going to start about paragraph 304. The mission involved several countries and we're going to see in due course that your report was a unanimous report; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Something itself of which you are proud.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you got there, what did you discover about the agreement that had already been forged by UNPROFOR? Paragraph 304.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we were debating the Resolution of the Security Council until midnight, thinking that we were about to preserve the safety of the people of Srebrenica, and when we got to Srebrenica, to Bosnia-Herzegovina, we found out that at the same time that we were debating this issue, the issue had already been settled on the ground; capitulation had been forced upon the Bosnian forces and demilitarisation and disarmament of the Bosnian side had started, implemented and enforced by UNPROFOR, which is much beyond the scope of the Resolution. But it meant that actually our Resolution was irrelevant and it was not pertinent because it had already been replaced by the action on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And again, the conflict between the public debate in the United Nations but the capitulation on the ground which we see reflected at tab 14 of the exhibits in the agreement which you've referred to, would that have been available to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go to paragraph 307, we're going to find that you prepared a report in due course. We shan't look at it in detail. In the course of that, you refer to the possibility of a massacre of 25.000 people having been stemmed by this agreement. Your view on whether that potential for massacre of 25.000 people was obvious at the time.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. It was a figure that we reached consulting with the representative UNHCR, the humanitarian office, the Red Cross, Medicins Sans Frontieres, and other NGOs plus the UNPROFOR forces on the ground, that was the estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say in the report that as the UNPROFOR agreement brings that to an end. What do you say as to whether that was the end of the threat or the risk of massacre of this number of people or whether it continued?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: At the moment, yes, because the whole attention of the international community, Your Honours, thanks fundamentally to the international media, we can focus on the case of Srebrenica and we thought at the moment a red light had been put on by the international media and public opinion at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the mid-term or long-term, however, what was the position?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: We thought, and it is in the report, that we saw crimen and the slow-motion genocide taking place and that a massacre would take place. And the degrading conditions when I visit Srebrenica were really unimaginable of the situation being suffered by the people in the area which had not been described to us and the Security Council at all. We thought that Srebrenica was under siege but never that it had been taken over it was like an open gaol where the -- this slow-motion genocide was taking place and was actually finalised in the second stage of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the risk to these people continue?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The risk continued because the UNPROFOR forces were actually under the control and supervision of the Serb paramilitary around the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to the detail in second. The risk continued. Was it obvious to you and to anybody on the ground --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, it was obvious that we were -- the whole village, enclave was surrounded by heavy weapons around the hills, we were shown that by UNPROFOR forces, and the Serb paramilitary were actually patrolling the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The -- the mission, paragraph 311, involved your being held up by a limited number of Serb soldiers for an hour and a half, I think, and having a gun pointed at you in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, it was five Serb soldiers stop about a contingent of about 20 armoured cars and a hundred paratroopers from Denmark that were escorting the Security Council mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did that and other events on the ground show you about who was in charge in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It was very clear to us that the United Nations was not in charge at all, that the Serbs were in charge, and the attitude of the officers who were leading us were like subordinates to the Serb soldiers, not even officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had that ever been revealed to you in New York?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Never. I mean, to me, to us, to the whole mission came as a shock so much so that even though some of the ambassadors who accompanied us and were part of the mission had a different position than the Security Council. They all signed the report and they noticed that that was the situation, and they were the ones who included this quotation in the report to the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Brigadier Hayes, who was your contact, facilitate your visit or did he stand in the way of your seeing what you wanted to see?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Brigadier Hayes was more interested in having sort of a perfunctory visit by the mission, not -- he did not show himself to be cooperative in any way to really get us to be able to discharge our responsibility in evaluating what was going on in Srebrenica. On the contrary; he did everything possible to block that we really get an impression. I would say that I understood finally why the United Nations didn't ever send missions to the ground, because when you send missions to the ground you find out the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think your colleagues were delayed and stalled. Everybody's cameras were taken away except yours, and yours were the only photographs broadcast around the world.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: That's the case. I was even brought into Zvornik without telling me. We landed in a stadium in Zvornik and I was greeted by the Serb colonel, Ratko I think was his name, who told me that I was arriving into the Republika Srpska, which of course we never recognise. And they -- I was held there for another hour. It was clear they were killing time for us not to get to Srebrenica, and my colleagues had been left behind in Kiseljak and actually arrived an hour later, and the journalists who came from New York international media were not allowed to come into Srebrenica. And the only -- the only camera that was allowed, because I didn't surrender, was mine and it was given to Reuters at the time and those were the photographs that came out of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then you saw Karadzic who'd previously said something about trapping the people in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, we saw the other indicted in Belgrade, in the airport in Belgrade. He was just coming out of a meeting with Mr. Milosevic, and that was at the airport when we met with him, and he had publicly said that they had them trapped like rats. And I actually quoted him in one of my speeches at the Security Council but we never anticipated what he meant until we got to Srebrenica and we really saw that he was not telling a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you made your complaints to him. Was this something he was expecting or was it, in your judgement, something that came as a surprise to him that complaints could be made in the way you did?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No, he was smiling all the time to us, you know. He didn't know anything. He didn't know that there was no water coming to the city, no electricity, no doctors --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: -- there were people starving, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To deal with the question of notice, you've described the control, the general atmosphere that was there. Page -- paragraph 344 on page 46. You then gave press statements which of course are available around the world, and to pick up some of them to save time, you've already dealt with the fact that this was a slow-motion genocide, that Srebrenica was far from being a safe area. You dealt with the cutting off of all aid, including medical aid, and you also said, is this correct, middle of paragraph 344, that there was open defiance of the international community?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you then made your observations later to some other journalists about, or perhaps Serbs running a concentration camp --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- policed by UNPROFOR. Meanwhile the slow-motion genocide to kill them gains speed.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we, to deal with the exhibits, look at tab 15, there's your unanimous report, and you set out a draft Resolution, which was not passed or was passed?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It was passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. You're dealing with the adopted Resolution first. But if we go on to the report, effectively the report itself, which is four pages in, under the heading "Situation on the Ground," you've set out a number of points. The Muslims viewed by the Serbs -- actions by the Muslims viewed by the Serbs as justifying their offensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Seven, the 70.000 people there. Down to paragraph 11, an account of how you'd been obstructed. Paragraph 13, your account of what Wahlgren told you that came as a surprise to you about the so-called agreement, or the agreement, rather. And then you set out the potential massacre of 25.000 people in paragraph 14. 17 you go back to that. 19 you deal with the slow-motion genocide. And then over the page, paragraph 27A, the town practically under siege -- sorry, 24 you set out what you observed, tanks dug in, heavy weapons, and so on; and 27A, under siege; B inhuman conditions. Over the page, G, the general humanitarian convoy position that you observed; K, the need to be kept fully informed. Was that document, your report, which can be perused in detail if necessary, available to the former Yugoslavia and to this accused?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Absolutely. That report was actually circulated to the whole General Assembly and it was widely quoted by the international media, Your Honours, so that definitely it was a very well known report. It was the first report ever produced by the Security Council on a mission on the ground during a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then we go through tabs 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22. They are samples of press and radio television output by you at that time?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your observations at the time, that this was a slow-motion genocide waiting to happen or in the course of happening, was that ever significantly challenged in the debate?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It was never challenged because it was so evident, Your Honours, to watch a small town surrounded by heavy weapons, no doctors coming in, no health, no water, no electricity, and it was obvious that it was going to be a matter of time, which unfortunately proved to be the case. And where the United Nations wasn't willing to do anything more forceful to prevent that from happening, not even with withdrawing the heavy weapons around the area or even allow the doctors to come into the area or water to be resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've described a state up and until your visit where information coming to New York was inadequate and indeed incorrect.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: And -- and not only that, usually late, too late. We -- we really, it was a tremendous great shock to all the members of the Security Council mission when we visit the area that the papers we had in our hands did not reflect the gravity and the tragic situation on the ground, and I think that that's why it propelled the members of the mission to put it in black and white and really present it to the Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your mission was able to bring -- put the problem of Srebrenica on the map for a time. Following this attempt of yours to bring change, what happened? Did the level of reporting and information coming out of Srebrenica continue at the higher level that you'd raised it to or did it return to the lower level?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It returned to the lower level, Your Honours. Not only that, at the time, the Secretary-General Boutros-Ghali addressed General Wahlgren on the ground to tell him that he didn't believe any military -- his interpretation of our Resolution did not imply any changes in the military attitude or policy. And that was corroborated to me by the Brigadier Hayes who told me in Sarajevo that the Security Council Resolution were woolly-headed Resolutions. If our own forces considered them irrelevant, you can remember what the Serbs in the area considered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you been able to effect any long-term change in any level of impunity existing in the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The Council never took any more measure -- initiative. The Canadian Battalion at the time was about 200 effective were left intact. They were not increased, augmented. The situation didn't change. What Mr. Karadzic offered to us at the Belgrade airport never took place, and the situation continued there, and other events continued absorbing the attention of the international media and Srebrenica slowly came out of the radar of the international community until it was too late and to -- in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 23, just to complete the documentary position. Tab 23 is a letter from the permanent representative of Pakistan dated the 14th of May, and this is a letter signed up by various people, the non-aligned group. It -- I think paragraph 2 says that the Council has been fundamentally unable to discharge its responsibilities under the Charter to maintain the collective security system as envisaged, has failed to redress this tragic situation. This is evident from the fact -- and then various facts are set out. Now, this document -- oh, yes. If we go over the page, please, to paragraph -- the top of page -- the next page, at the end of what is paragraph 4. "Since the London International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia and up to the Vance-Owen Plan, the Serbs have repeatedly deceived the international community and reneged on their commitments. The Serbs have used the negotiating process and the Vance-Owen Plan not as a means to a peaceful solution but as a vehicle for procrastination and for gaining internationally legitimacy." Was that the view held by your group at that time?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If I may explain something that I believe is very significant: The non-aligned countries in the Security Council were very concerned that all these debates were taking place in a closed room. People always to used to see the public room of the Security Council, but in formal consultation room, which are where the real debates and discussions are held, were not being made public. And the non-aligned felt that the real questions were not being brought up to the light. That was reason that we produced this document, which became then and gave the full information not only what was our position but what our information was regarding this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So again available to the former Yugoslavia, and at paragraph 15 on the same document: "Bosnia and Herzegovina have become a symbol of the resistance to the resurgence of the crime of genocide," and you set out more than a hundred thousand deaths, and you say, "No one can claim ignorance or lack of knowledge of these facts."

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Even in colours, there was -- the only crime that wasn't committed there was the crime of silence, like Bertrand Russell once said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then tab 24, Resolution 827, adopted on the 25th of May, does alarm -- continue to express alarm at continuing the talks of genocide. And then finally, the tab is tab 25, a number of countries dealing with -- a draft Resolution this. Just tell us about this, please.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: This was a draft Resolution which we presented to lift the arms embargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Described, as I explained before in my previous comments, to really provide to -- to one of the parties the capacity to defend itself, which is enshrined in the United Nations charter, because we were negating them the possibility to defend them so at least we should allow them to defend themselves. And even though that was a unanimous decision by the General Assembly, it did not get the support of the permanent members of the Security Council with exception of the United States who supported our proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just got a couple of more questions, with your leave, and then I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the draft statement, acting as an aide-memoire, at page 60, paragraph 436, you set out how it was that it was on the 29th of June that you spoke in favour of the draft Resolution that you advanced, and at page 400 -- page 64, paragraph 463, some of the things you said, which were of course going to be reported back to Belgrade in your judgement, you set out how the UN was not a debating Chamber. You likened the position there to Czechoslovakia in 1938. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you said that the historical backdrop, page -- paragraph 465: "... had sowed many dangerous seeds in the degenerating conflict. President Izetbegovic has been called intransigent by Lord Owen, just as Benes was. And Bosnia-Herzegovina is being compelled to cede to its Croat and Serb neighbours 90 per cent of its territory. What will be left will be perfectly homogenous areas within the spirit of apartheid so often condemned by this organisation." You go on to extend your analogy with Czechoslovakia, and at paragraph 467 you set out the danger of preventing people from the right to defend themselves. Mr. Arria, as you know the time is limited and I have indeed exhausted my time: You did everything you could, or did you do everything you could to describe the position on the ground to the world and to the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir, even though I believe it was completely unnecessary because the whole world knew what was taking place. It was being recorded, Your Honours, by all the international media and television all over the world, so what we did was to add I would say the gravity of coming from the Security Court members as the non-aligned members of the Security Council agreed. By the way, I don't think add anything new except when, during our visit to Srebrenica, Your Honours, when we found this dire and terrible and tragic situation. Otherwise, the whole world knew exactly what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the means of communication that you've described identified the risk to the 25.000 people that you set out in your report?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Absolutely. I remember perfectly well, Your Honours, even The New York Times carrying a long story about what slow-motion genocide meant and actually fatally happened in 1995. It was an accumulation. I always believe that the massacre started in 1993. It did not take place, started in 1995. It was the same crime in an accumulated fashion that just took a longer period to be implemented and executed but it was a massacre that started two years and it took two years to accomplish and went beyond the 7.000 people of Srebrenica. It was around 20.000, even according to the report of Secretary-General Kofi Annan on the Srebrenica report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the absence of a red light, to which you referred at the very beginning, was that clear to those who became involved in this matter?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I always believed that the sense of the culture, Your Honours, of impunity started when the United Nations, the UNPROFOR forces were taken to the airport in Sarajevo. The Deputy Prime Minister of Bosnia, Mr. Turajlic, they opened the door of an armoured car and he was murdered in front of a patrol of United Nations troops and no one did raise a finger, did anything about it, and it was clear that if you can murder, with the protection of the United Nations, the Deputy Prime Minister the newest member of the United Nations, you can get away with murder, which actually they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the indulgence of a few more minutes, but I hope that's a compact form of evidence acceptable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. The Chamber is grateful for your cooperation. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, how much time am I going to have for the cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We had originally indicated one hour, but in view of the examination-in-chief, we'll give you an hour and 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I received this witness's statement, which is almost 500 paragraphs long, last night, and I received your decision that his presentation would be shorter, shortened, and that Mr. Nice would have 30 minutes. Mr. Nice took up 60 minutes, as you've just seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. He has used only 40 minutes, 41 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, commence. The Chamber has always been sensitive to your right to cross-examine. If you have an application to make at the end, then you can make it and we'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Arria, in paragraph 7 of your statement you say the following: "This statement is not meant to provide a definitive chronology [In English] of events relating to all matters I dealt with as I was brought in and out of service of the UN Security Council. I have been asked by staff from the Office of the Prosecutor -- I have been asked by staff from the office of Prosecutor to review a number of documents and comment on them." [Interpretation] That's a quotation from your statement. Was that indeed the task you were given by the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you adhere to the task presented in that way when you made your statement?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The request to me, Your Honours, was not regimented my contribution to my position. I volunteer most of the information that is provided in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you selected the information; is that right? The information that you provided and the comments you provided.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I always had full control of my own contribution to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Arria, but the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a continuous process, and the Security Council followed the continuity of this process. Do you feel that a complete picture of this process and UN Security Council reactions can be given if you limit your analysis to just a part of the documents without giving us a full chronology of the events?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: That was precisely, Your Honours, what I tried to contribute to the case, to fill the gaps that were -- have to be filled and to bring exactly whole context of my experience throughout whole process in the Security Council and not -- that's what I said. I was not regimented or limited in my contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But Mr. Arria, when we're talking about the events that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you weren't present, you weren't there, you have no direct knowledge of them with the exception of your brief stay there in April 1993 within the frameworks of the UN Security Council mission; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: We had the information from many sources, not only from our own, Your Honours, visit. We had, even though some of them were late, we had from the UNPROFOR forces, we had from the missions who had people on the ground, so we had -- we were in a privileged position to really know and to get information, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I say that you have no direct knowledge except that brief stay from the 23rd to the 26th of April, that's what I mean, that's right, isn't it? And during those three days, you visited Zagreb and Belgrade and various other places in Bosnia. So your immediate direct knowledge was only based on what you learnt during the space of those three days. Isn't that right, Mr. Arria?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, that's not the case. There have been many reports from commission of experts, human rights, the UN, especially the United Nations Human Rights Commission, special commission, et cetera, there was a lot of information. Of course you cannot have access directly to all of them, but we were receiving a lot of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in fact, you are testifying only about what you learnt and the information you received from other sources, in fact. Would that be right, Mr. Arria?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No. I am relying on my own information. I'm relying on information from reliable sources, qualified sources to report to Security Council. After all, the Security Council doesn't have people on the ground. The whole United Nations system is actually politically under the Security Council, so actually, Your Honours, we were working with the whole system that is supposedly working for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So that means that you as the representative of Venezuela in the UN Security Council at that time base your knowledge on the events on the ground from reports that were sent out by representatives of UNPROFOR in the field, or UNMO, and it was their task to follow events in the area and to report back to New York; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No, not necessarily the case. We received information, Your Honours, like I said before, from different sources, missions, the commission of experts, the UNPROFOR, our own mission on the ground, our own embassies, embassies from other countries that had access to information. So it was -- we were not lacking, from that point of view, information what was really happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Arria, in paragraph 38 of your statement, you say the following: "I always thought that the UN Security Council, [In English] regardless of its international political prominence was collectively an extremely poorly informed body for two reasons. First because the permanent members generally do not share information available to them; and second, because the secretariat reports were regularly late and often partial and incomplete and not necessarily because of the ignorance of the facts." [Interpretation] So it was this information precisely to which you are referring that you say in paragraph 38 were withheld and that the UN Security Council was an extremely poorly informed body is what you say.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Security Council officially, that's what I mean, was poorly informed but not in the reality. The problem with the Security Council was precisely that they don't want to acknowledge and they won't recognise even though they knew what was taking place. So it wasn't because of lacking of information. What I meant was a lack of official information that could be acted upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Arria, but the first of the reasons that you indicate was not that all the persons were not informed but the permanent members generally do not share information with others. And then in paragraph 29, you say that the permanent members had their own sources of information and that it was those -- that they shared those informations with the -- selectively and at their convenience shared the information. It was the non-permanent members that were not informed or, rather, their representatives.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but again I reinstate it was officially but in reality we knew, there were a lot of people in the United Nations membership countries who were alarmed what was happening on the ground and were willing to provide information to us, even missions from the permanent member countries, from the permanent members of the Security Council. So we had ample information to act. What -- but there was not officially acknowledged by some of the permanent members who really didn't want to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The fact that you accuse these UN Security Council members is your affair, but you say that the secretariat, and I'm quoting you, "The secretariat reports were regularly late and often partial and incomplete. [In English] And not necessarily because of the ignorance of the facts." [Interpretation] So Ghali and his services consciously and intentionally covered up the facts. Is that what you're saying, Mr. Arria, in fact?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's only one accused party here. I'm not accusing anybody else except the accused. And then what I said that, that also -- I consider this operation one of the most -- the greatest cover-up operation of the United Nations officially because so much information was kept away from the -- from the Security Council membership to act upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The -- there's a very narrow area of relevance of the evidence of this witness, and that is why the Chamber issued an order directing the Prosecutor how to conduct the examination-in-chief. The United Nations and the Security Council is, of course, not on trial here, but what happened there is -- is important and relevant as part of the backdrop, the background to the events in Srebrenica. I understand Mr. Milosevic to be asking you about the -- how well the Security Council was informed, because to the extent that it was poorly informed and that you are a member, then he might be saying that you're also poorly informed, and I think that is what you need to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I fully grasp the meaning of the accused's remarks and questions to me, and I would like to try to clarify what I said, that officially the Council was very poorly informed, but that didn't mean that the members of the Council would not get access to the information except for information that we were only able to gather on the ground, like during our visit to Srebrenica. I don't know whether I make myself clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have been trying to establish that this witness presented the facts in a lopsided manner, upside down. He is criticising the Security Council and the Secretary-General, and it seems the Security Council did not know anything, but it seems that the entire UN structure, only he and a few member of his group knew something and that no one else knew a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Arria, in paragraph 29 you even went a step further in your accusations against Boutros-Ghali. You say [In English]: "... in some cases has provided disinformation." [Interpretation] You emphasised that far the case with Bosnia-Herzegovina and specifically Srebrenica. So you claim not only that the secretariat headed by Boutros Boutros-Ghali denied you information but that even they disinformed you that they gave you misinformation. That is a major accusation, isn't it? I'm quoting you, so that is what you allege.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is very clear to me that I'm not accusing anybody else except the accused. The -- the relevance of this -- of the secretariat not providing information on time or it is very clear -- I actually mention in Madame Ogata's letter, for example, of October -- October -- March 18, I only came to see this letter 11 years later. If that's not misinformation, it's very difficult to understand what misinformation means. Not only that, we were prevented -- actually the Secretary-General at the time, Boutros-Ghali was almost never present during the private consultations when we were debating the position of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was very critical of this arm-length position from the man who is responsible to the charge and moral responsibility, like the case of the Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is time for a break. We are I think five minutes beyond. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I raise an entirely separate administrative matter that it would be helpful to sort out just now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let me have the witness now leave. We're going to break for half an hour, and during the break you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody. You may leave, Mr. Arria.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Small matter. The Court will remember issuing an order about a range of documents, SDC minutes, Council for Harmonisation documents and so on in respect of which it seeks us to provide and we are going to provide analysis and interpretation. The task is a rather large one and despite staff working all weekend, I'd be grateful for a short extension of time. The Chamber may remember that there's a return date for the amici I think one month after our document is in, and if you could give us until the end of the week that would be of great assistance to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's granted. Yes. We adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Arria, let it be quite clear. I am fully challenging your assertion that the general secretary of the UN at the time, that is to say Boutros-Ghali, misinformed you and that when you say the secretary in some cases, that is a completely unfounded accusation levelled against the then-Secretary-General. Are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe if that will be the case, I think Mr. Boutros-Ghali would choose another lawyer besides the accused.
