utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your answer. I'm quoting you, Mr. Arria, because you say: "Has provided disinformation."

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also express a lack of confidence in the Secretary-General and the Security Council and everybody except for what you have been saying all along yourself in terms of what you say happened.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the accused referred before to a group, I would like to tell you that our group meant 110 countries in the United Nations, all the non-aligned countries of the United Nations, whom the members of the non-aligned who were represented in the Security Council kept always in consultation. So it was not only the opinion of only five members or non-aligned members of the Security Council. To illustrate to the Court, Your Honour, you allow me, I will tell you only three things which I didn't want to extend more. Mrs. Ogata was the highest official of the United Nations in charge of humanitarian refugees. On March 18th informed the Secretary-General of the emerging tragedy of an imminent danger for the population of Srebrenica. It took two weeks for the Secretary-General to inform the Security Council. The night that we were debating the Security Council Resolution of safe areas, the secretariat knew fully well that Srebrenica had already been capitulated, even though they did not inform the Council that such-and-such was the case. The third case, when the new Resolution for all the safe areas, the secretariat withdrew the terms of reference that had been prepare by Madame Ogata and the secretariat itself which were excellent terms of reference to really create safe areas, they were withdrawn by the secretariat at the instruction of the Secretary-General. That was what I was -- when I address the issue of the lack of cooperation or misinformation or cover-up, this is what I'm referring to, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Arria, since you mentioned Mrs. Ogata now and her letter that you showed here, are you aware of the fact that it was actually the other way round, that it was quite different from what you've been trying to say all along as you show this letter, because she says: "[In English] During the course of three telephone conversations I had with President Milosevic on passage of relief convoys to Eastern and Central Bosnia, and in particular to Srebrenica." [Interpretation] Do you know that there has not been a single case whatsoever that Serbia and I personally, and I was the one whom Mrs. Ogata addressed, turned a deaf ear to requests put forth by the UN High Commissioner for Refugees in order to facilitate the passage of humanitarian convoys? Every humanitarian convoy that went through Serbia was approved and not a single one was prevented from carrying out their mission. You do not have one single case that Serbia presented any kind of obstacle to humanitarian aid. On the contrary. Serbia made every effort to make it possible for humanitarian convoys to come through. Do you know that Serbia itself sent convoys to Serbia, including Sarajevo, including the Muslims in Sarajevo? So what have you been trying to prove through this letter as far as Serbia's concerned and as far as I'm concerned personally? You do not have a single case that we did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must allow the witness to answer the question that you have raised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I sort of understood that was a statement rather than a question. I don't know -- will you please correct me if that's wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the substance of his question is that Serbia did not present any kind of obstacle to humanitarian convoys coming through.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Serbia provided all the tanks, ammunition, armament, uniforms, fuel to precisely to their proxies who were preventing the humanitarian assistance to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is an absurd assertion, Mr. Arria, but let's move on. You say in connection with this lack of information which is impermissible, and you say that it was Boutros-Ghali and his services. In paragraph 30 you say: "[In English] The filter became excessive in the case of the former Yugoslavia tragedy when the filter turned into a dam for the containment of information that limited and prevented the arrival of valuable information to Security Council in realtime, even on issues affecting the lives of thousands of peoples." [Interpretation] Are you accusing the secretariat or, rather, Boutros-Ghali of having committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the documents that I presented, General Wahlgren admits that a month before we ever knew that Srebrenica was about to fall the secretariat knew about it. That's precisely what I'm referring to. The information was not provided in time. I hardly doubt that the Security Council would have done much more had it been provided information but the situation was not as dire a month before as it was in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to Ghali, you spare no accusations, even in insulting terms. Paragraph 42 when you say that he did not come to informal consultations at the UN. You call Ghali's behaviour "[In English] perverse to define such a practice." "I can only use the term perverse to define such a practice."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the specific question that you're putting to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that Ghali was concealing information and providing misinformation about things that had to do with the lives of thousands of people and that he behaved in a perverse way? You describe the behaviour of the General-Secretary at the request of a body which aspires to be a body of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, almost 11 years ago I raised my hand to approve the creation of this Tribunal, and it was precisely to handle the case such as the person who is the accused, not to consider the Secretary-General. So I have said in my deposition, and I repeat it, that at the time I always was critical and I remain very critical of the lack of candidness, to use a term, by the secretariat and some of the member countries to admit and to provide the real information in realtime to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Arria. You are no less harsh in an assessing the behaviour of envoys in negotiations, like Cyrus Vance and Lord David Owen. In paragraph 148 of your statement, you say: "[In English] Negotiations were ongoing at the time under the leadership of David Owen and Cyrus Vance. A territorial division of an apartheid character was being proposed by them and by Milosevic ..." So according what you say, the two of them, together with me, created apartheid in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is a crime, isn't it? How did you get that idea?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The Security Council, the non-members, Your Honour, always said that it was -- it should not be the outcome that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be divided apartheid lines, which precisely the United Nations fought for years before. One of the greatest victories of the United Nations was the victory against apartheid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic is, however, asking what is the specific basis for your conclusion that he was proposing a division based on apartheid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the accused was at -- proceeded -- adopted a policy of endless conversations and negotiations with the Security Council with some of the mediators. I was perfectly informed by Mr. Owen and Mr. Vance at the time precisely of what the ambitions of the Serb Party were. At the time, even included from the beginning Srebrenica as part of what they called later on the Republika Srpska. That's what I'm referring to. And it came -- that part came from Mr. Milosevic himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even that is not correct, that it came directly from me. And I asked you a question by quoting you directly, because you say territorial division of an apartheid character was being proposed by them. So it's Owen and Cyrus Vance. And then you add "and by Milosevic." That's why I'm telling you, so the two of them, together with me, created some kind of an apartheid.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I think I already replied, Your Honour, to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know, Mr. Arria, that the Vance-Owen Plan precisely envisaged the cantonisation of Bosnia, which hardly overlapped with the ethnic pattern of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Partly it did coincide, but partly it did not at all. So that was not the basic premise of the Vance-Owen Plan that we all supported, to create any kind of apartheid. After all that, plan still exists and can be seen.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, precisely the part that did not coincide on ethnic grounds was the area of Srebrenica, and I think that the main party in this conflict knows what they did about it, which was precisely to remove the people from Srebrenica which were far away from Sarajevo. That's precisely the region that did not fit exactly into the ethnic partition. Srebrenica was the part that paid for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Arria, in paragraphs 150, 51 and 52 of your statement you say: "[In English] The surrender of Srebrenica to the Serbs was of strategic importance - both for the Serbs and for the UN negotiators - because Srebrenica had to be in Serb-held territory in order to be able to secure a peace 'deal.' "It would become part of Greater Serbia. "Such a premeditated course of action can be easily established by just following the reports that Secretary-General Boutros-Ghali never shared with the Council non-permanent members - who were the only ones who would have opposed such a course - as well as by reading the directives he provided to UNPROFOR not to assist in the protection of the enclaves." [Interpretation] So this is what you said in terms of the responsibility of the UN negotiators. I assume that you include Owen in addition to Vance and the Secretary-General and the permanent members of the Security Council. So this is a premeditated course of action, as you put it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I have even put it in writing what's my position, which I don't want it to be altered in the way that's been presented by Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't alter anything, Mr. Arria. I just quoted you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In other words, you stand by what is in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in your opinion, Owen, Vance, and the Security Council, together with me, created some kind of a basis for a Greater Serbia. Is that what you're alleging? There's a lack of seriousness in that, Mr. Arria. Doesn't it look that way to you?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No, it doesn't look that way at all to me. From the first negotiations, at the end, the outcome that came from the peace Resolution at the end of the conflict reflected precisely what was intended from the beginning, which was an ethnic partition of Bosnia which unfortunately took place at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying now that the Dayton Agreement was also misconceived, the one that brought the war in Bosnia to an end, achieved peace? Is that what you're claiming, Mr. Arria?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how the accused feels about it. I feel greatly relieved that fortunately peace was brought to people with whom he humiliated and damaged for such a long time but I don't think that is the cause of issue that is at stake, but if you want me to reply to that, Your Honour, I will do that with pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But please take a look at paragraph 46 of your statement, the UN mission. You say -- you actually refer to the enclaves, the safe areas, and then you say: "[In English] But in any Resolution to give effect to such designation, it should be clearly and emphatically recorded that the establishment Security Council safe areas in no way -- in no way undermines the proposed settlement details of the --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think we're having difficulty finding that. Did you say paragraph 46?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in the report of the mission to the Security Council. His mission or, rather, the mission of his group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "[In English] ... in no way undermines the proposed settlement details of the Vance-Owen Plan. It is not an attempt to create new and different internal boundaries within Bosnia." [Interpretation] So you, like all members of the mission then, supported the Vance-Owen Plan. Does that mean that by giving your support in writing by way of an official document, you supported apartheid, actually, by way of supporting the creation of a Greater Serbia? Because in this report of yours, you actually support the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I couldn't follow the paragraph that he's quoting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he's referring to paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not paragraph 46 of your statement but paragraph 46 of the report to the Security Council. Mr. Nice, is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's tab 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tab 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And page 11.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 46. I have it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you read the paragraph, and are you in a position now to answer the question raised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, Your Honour, I am. Throughout the whole process, the non-aligned members of the -- we always endorse all peace plans that were proposed, especially the Vance-Owen Plan. It was always -- we could not but hope for peace, but at the same time we were demanding some force of action would be taken by the Security Council and we conceived that to be compatible and especially compatible with the political situation within the Security Council, which nothing else could be achieved. And unfortunately, I believe at the end the Council agreement brought, as actually corroborated, the ending partition of a country, setting a terrible precedent for humanity. I believe so, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that you're not testifying here about your convictions, but it has become obvious that you are testifying about your convictions. So you supported the Vance-Owen Plan, although you said before that the Vance-Owen Plan was -- or, rather, that Vance and Owen, together with me, were creating a division which constituted apartheid. That plan, if you don't know that, Mr. Arria, was made by the three parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Yugoslavia supported that as it supported all other peace plans. In that respect, you cannot find any difference between the positions upheld by the Security Council and the positions of Yugoslavia, because Yugoslavia, Serbia, and I personally supported all peace plans. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I am very much aware, Your Honour, that Srebrenica was always an issue in discussion, because the Serb side always wanted to have Srebrenica, which was -- they wanted to have it always on the Serb side, and that was finally what happened. Srebrenica today is on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these maps are the result of the final negotiations held in Dayton on the basis of the finally adopted position which was based on the proposal of the Contact Group, 51 to 49 between Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that proposal of the Contact Group had been put forth months before that. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment of Dayton, already the situation created by the atrocities committed by the Serb side in Bosnia-Herzegovina have settled already the issue. There was no option for the Bosnia-Herzegovina government to accept those terms, especially knowing that no one else was going to do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Arria, since you were not in Dayton, you probably don't know that all options were on the table, and there weren't any questions that were reserved, so to speak, and that could not be discussed. The Dayton Agreement is the result of consensus among the three parties that participated in it as well as the representatives of the Contact Group and the host country, the United States. I assume that you know that and that you don't need me to explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether the Council will -- the Dayton Agreement is part of what you would like me to consider in the time that I've been given. If you want me to, I will go into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, answer to the extent that you can, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stand by what I said before. I believe that at the outcome it was -- people had already been ravaged, the country has been destroyed, subject to genocide, all kinds of crimes against humanity, and the situation settled by the Serb forces with the support of Belgrade had made it -- that possible, and there were no other options but the representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina to sign. There are many books written about what happened there, and I'm sure Your Honours know about it, but there is one item, a fact that remains standing, that at the end, Bosnia-Herzegovina, one of the newest countries of the United Nations, partitioned on ethnic considerations, and that's -- I -- I stand on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Arria. You stand by facts that cannot be corroborated in the field, actually, but let us move on, because our time is not unlimited. In paragraph 35, you say: "[In English] The non-permanent members therefore often relied on media sources rather than UN information services. They were usually more reliable than the secretariat ..." [Interpretation] So since you were very poorly informed in the Security Council, you received information from the media; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, if a courageous British photographer and journalist had not brought to the attention of the world what was happening in Srebrenica even though the United Nations knew, we didn't know, all the attention would have been provided, and it was international media precisely in Great Britain that provided that information. The media was following actually were the greatest allies that the non-permanent members had. They had more people on the ground covering up and being objective and independently providing information. That was not the only source, of course, but it was the one that resounded more in public opinion. Srebrenica to a great extent was not massacre in April 1993 because of the assistance that this British journalist provided to world opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why there was not a massacre in 1993 is something that is clearly testified about. There is a lot of evidence about that, but I'm not going to take up any more time because you obviously don't know about it. If you received your information from the media, can one therefore infer that you did not differ substantially from millions of people who received their information by watching television, listening to the radio, and reading the newspapers? Can we, therefore, conclude that you are no better a witness than any other listener of the radio or any other person who read the newspapers, watched television, and so on?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, had it not been for this information, General Morillon probably would not have appeared in Srebrenica, and he did. And when you compound the news that were circulating in the world and immediately General Morillon going to Srebrenica, that made it impossible for the Security Council not to meet. And I must tell Your Honours that had it not been because the non-aligned countries present their Resolution to create a safe area, no Resolution had been created, probably just a presidential statement would have only been circulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not true, but as we'll have occasion to hear General Morillon here in this courtroom, I don't suppose there's any need for you to testify in place of General Morillon. Now, tell me, please, since you're speaking about the media and the fact that you were informed thereof, do you agree with the observation made by David Owen which he presents in his book, and I'm going to quote from that book, and it is linked to the media. This is what he says: "In this stage of the propaganda war via its relations with the public has become a feature of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The documents registered with the Ministry of Justice of the United States of America have shown that the -- that Croatia paid a Washington company for relations with the public, Rudder-Finn Global Public, $10.000 a month plus expenses, for it to project a favourable image of Croatia, a member of the Congress, the function of administration and media placing news, and for their part the Bosnian government paid for services rendered in placing comments and columns by writers to -- and letters to the editor." And then it goes on it state all the activities undertaken. I haven't got time to quote Lord Owen in full on all these communiques, interviews and all the rest granted to the press through official letters and so on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We must now put a specific -- you must now put a specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Lord Owen concludes that: "In the International Committee for the Former Yugoslavia we did not have the means by which to respond to something of that nature." So he means to this media propaganda that Owen is indicating. So are you bearing that in mind or not, and do you agree with him or don't you?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that's for Lord Owen to respond to himself. I cannot respond for Lord Owen, but I can make, if you like, a couple of comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you wish to, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will. Had Belgrade not been under sanction most probably would have also hired a public relation firm but they were under sanction. Had the former Yugoslavia kept the prestige it had for many years until this conflict started, they would not have needed any kind of public relations to help them. Yugoslavia was, before the accused came in, a very respected and prestigious country in the international community. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, why, then, did the Bosnian government need experts for public relations and paid agitators and lobbyists in Congress and in the media in general in the west? Why did they need that if everything you say was true?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, I'm not here to -- first, I'm not privy to what Bosnia had or had not. That's for them to respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But bearing in mind the propaganda war that Lord Owen mentions, can you say with certainty that the media information upon which you based your knowledge about the events in Bosnia were always true and correct and reliable?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot comment on the propaganda war. What I can comment is on the ethnic cleansing war, on the massacre war, and the crimes and atrocities being committed. That I can report. I cannot report on the propaganda war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, since in the report that I quoted from, and it is your own report I was quoting, paragraph 46, whereas we can see you say nice things about the Vance-Owen Plan, whereas in the statement you gave following an assignment from the opposite side you say the worst things about the peace plan. So what knowledge did you gain in the meantime which influenced this change of opinion on your part?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Repeat the question and clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Arria, in your statement, the one that I quoted from, saying nice things about the plan, and you gave that statement at the request of the opposite side, meaning Mr. Nice. Now, in your report you say favourable things about that same Vance Plan. So I'm asking you now, from the time you made favourable statements about the plan, what made you change your opinion? What influences were you working under which led you to change your opinion about the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The behaviour of the accused fundamentally, the systematic boycotting of the process, the creation of the image that the accused was going to -- being the main party was really going to be put into effect, the finalisation of the conflict. That's what created fundamentally our change of opinion and policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Arria, it is common knowledge that all my efforts, and you say that that is the main side, geared -- was geared towards achieving peace, and nobody can dispute that through all the peace plans that were put on the negotiating table. Are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: We were clear that the two-prong approach had been adopted by the Serbian side. One side you had the accused, Mr. Milosevic, entertaining endless negotiation. On the other side you had his proxies on the ground doing the dirty work of the ethnic cleansing and killing, committing atrocities, and that two-prong approach was led the international community to wait for so many years and almost 200.000 people to be killed and dead until they finally reacted and put an end to this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, come on, Mr. Arria. You're talking about our relationship towards ethnic cleansing. I'm going to quote now something from 1992. So the year is 1992, much before you yourself were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you quoting from, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my interview given to the ITN TV network where I speak about the London conference, and I say that we are associating our efforts to stop the bloody events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then I go on to say the following: "There are some," I say that, "there are some who are advocating some sort of ethnic cleansing, and I say to that we in Serbia consider that that is a criminal act, a crime." And that was in the summer of 1992. Officially we emphasised very clearly that something like that must not happen and that anybody engaging in things of that kind must be prosecuted criminally. And then I go on to speak about Bosnia and say that there is a civil war going on there and in wars like that there are no innocent sides and victors. All there are are casualties and victims. So the London conference held in the summer of 1992, then, is what I mention, and you say that we behaved as if we did not know about this and did not wish to help to bring about peace. So what I read out was my statement to the British ITN news network, and it refers precisely to those who, as it says here, are advocating ethnic cleansing. And my position was that we in Serbia consider that to be a crime, a criminal act, and any perpetrators thereof must be brought to justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know this detail, for example? Are you aware of that detail, Mr. Arria? And that is just one of the examples that I chose to quote, but there are many others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness answer, now, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my only comment to this would be that I only wish that he had lived up to these words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, for example, Mr. Arria, that the first crimes or criminal acts that people learnt about, the crimes that took place in Bosnia and where it was established that the perpetrators were certain citizens of Serbia or those who were in fact taken to court and tried for war crimes in Serbia in 1993? They were prosecuted. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't just verbally, it was the actual factual conduct of Serbia this should not be allowed. And as you know the former Yugoslavia, Mr. Arria, and are well acquainted with Serbia and Montenegro, I assume you know that throughout the ten years that the crisis lasted it was only Serbia and Montenegro which did not change anything in the ethnic structure and that nobody was persecuted in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on an ethnic basis in any way whatsoever. Do you know about that? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that that one -- that single case contradicts what I said before. I only wish and hope that Mr. Milosevic would have lived up to what he declare, like he declare many other times and he would do something about it. And it took many years. And it took until the international community regain resolve and will to really force Mr. Milosevic to put an end to this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Arria, well, I assume that it was a civil war between three warring parties in Bosnia and not Mr. Milosevic's war, as you said. And Lord Owen wrote about it anyway, and he spoke about it too. It was a civil war between the Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Serbs, and Bosnian Croats, the three sides. And as opposed to you, he was there all the time, and throughout he was at the head of the international conference.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, if this had been a civil war like the accused is stating, his country would have never been under sanctions. His country would have never been mentioned in more than 50 Resolutions. Why would former Yugoslavia be punished by the international community if this was a civil war? This was not a civil war. It was war of aggression of one former member of the United Nations against a smaller undefended member of the United Nations. This was not civil war. This was a war of aggression, conquers of territory, ethnic cleansing. That's what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As for the nature of the conflict, that is a legal issue which the Chamber will have to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you say that the sanctions were introduced because Yugoslavia behaved as it should not have behaved, I'm going to remind you of something now. The statement or, rather, report of the UN Secretary-General linked to a UN Security Council Resolution number 752. This is the 30th of May, 1992. I think I received it within the batch of documents I was given, report of the Secretary-General, pursuant to paragraph 4 of the Security Council Resolution number 752.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just allow us to find it, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice, can you help us? Or maybe Mr. Milosevic himself can tell us. Do you have the tab number, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 4.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have a lot of papers here. It was in one of the tabs, and I pulled it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... he's referring to, the proposal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to try tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The way he describes it, it makes it a little unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, it doesn't appear to be tab 4. If he shows me the document or if he shows Ms. Dicklich the document, we can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I tell you what, Mr. Milosevic, you continue with your cross-examination. Just read very slowly the passage, and I'm quite sure we will be able to gather what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 12 of the witness statement of Dr. Arria contains a reference to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kay. Page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, this is a report of the UN Secretary-General, and I'm just going to read a couple -- or, rather, three basic points that I wish to refer to. This is what he says, and it is the report of Boutros-Ghali to the UN Security Council on the 30th of May, 1992. Point 5 says: "[In English] The bulk of the JNA personnel were deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina were citizens of that republic and were not therefore covered by Belgrade authorities' decision of 4th of May to withdraw JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Most of them appear to have joined army of so-called Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Others have joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina which is under the political control of the Presidency of that republic. Others may have joined various irregular forces operating there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Time to put your question now, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Point 6 reads: "[In English] [Previous translation continues]... citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina are said by the Belgrade authorities number barely 20 per cent of the total. Most of these are believed to have withdrawn already into Serbia and Montenegro, some of them having been subjected to attack during their withdrawal. Others, however, remain at the various garrison in Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially in Serb-controlled areas, et cetera. A further category consists of personnel who have been blocked -- personnel who have been blocked in their barracks by the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina or hostile irregular forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's now time for you to put a question. Otherwise, the sense of the original passages will have been lost.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Arria, is it clear to you that in the UN Secretary-General's report, Boutros-Ghali to the Security Council, it clearly states that the decision of the leadership of Yugoslavia was to withdraw its citizens because at the time Bosnia-Herzegovina had already been recognised. And Yugoslavia does that. It withdraws all its citizens who were members of the Yugoslav People's Army from Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the people who were not withdrawn were those who were blocked in some of the garrisons and couldn't be. I assume that's clear to you.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not been able to find this in my documents. What I have found is the other counterpart of the present Secretary-General for United Nations's report to Srebrenica, which is the opposite to what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you need it to be able to answer the question, you need to see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I want to make sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You want to make sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that's what was said because Mr. Annan said something completely different in his report on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we're not able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last document we thought we'd found as Exhibit 547, tab 2, but that's the Resolution. The latest document, I'm not sure what's being referred to, if the same or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have the document there?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is, yes. And I was quoting from that document, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the usher pass it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have it back, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think the witness will purloin it, Mr. Milosevic. Will you just pass it to the witness and let the witness read it, the particular passages. I am now told it's Defence Exhibit 91. After the witness has read it, Mr. Milosevic will rephrase his question very shortly, and the witness will answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, meanwhile I can tell you this is the first time ever I see this document and the title on top is different to the regular documents of the Security Council. So I don't even know who issued this. Doesn't look like an official document of the Security Council at all. Doesn't have a number, doesn't have a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Pass it to me. I do have some familiarity with Security Council Resolutions. It seems to be a report of the Secretary-General pursuant to a Security Council Resolution. That's Exhibit 91. And, Mr. Milosevic, you are quoting from what paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Point 5, para 5, I believe, Mr. Robinson. If you turn the page and have a look at paragraph 5, and I think 6 and 7 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Would you pass that to the witness. I have marked it. It's on the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may I be given my own copy back, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Give Mr. Milosevic his copy. So it's a report of the Secretary-General pursuant to a Resolution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The one I was presented was a different text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one I also recognise. I've never seen it before, I must tell you. On the -- precisely on that point, Your Honour, the Secretary-General Kofi Annan's report on Srebrenica states specifically that the bulk of the army suddenly created by sort of an act of magic in the so-called Republika Srpska was coming from Belgrade. The Secretary-General Annan says himself that also with people linked to Mafia and criminal activities were the ones, are the way he described it in his now well-known report on Srebrenica. And he says here, in a way he's in contradiction because this initial report by Secretary-General Annan says it is a mission on the responsibility of the United Nations failing a member country. And I'm just quoting Mr. Annan's words. And he says the opposite of this. He says precisely that they were transferred, ammunition, tanks, planes, radars, the whole thing was transferred from Belgrade. It was not an act of magic. It was an act of support by Belgrade to create these armed forces to the group that was the same coming from Serbia. Now, whether there were some from Bosnia -- Bosnia was an ecumenical country until this conflict began. There were all kinds of ethnic groups living under the same roof until they were provoked into this conflict. So I see, Your Honour, differences between Secretary-General Boutros-Ghali's remarks, which is the first time I see this document, and the Secretary-General Kofi Annan several years later evaluating the situation, stating perfectly clear that they moved the armed forces from Serbia, from former Yugoslavia, to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, whether they were -- of course there must have been contingents of these officers who were already living on the other side. After all, it used to be one country until the year before. That's all I have to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Arria, let's be proper in our conduct and stick to the report from those times, that is to say when Boutros-Ghali, on the 30th of May, 1992, reported to the United Nations Security Council. And it is quite clear in that report that those parts of the JNA - and as you know, it was an army throughout the territory of Yugoslavia - that those people that originated from Serbia and Montenegro or, rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, were being withdrawn to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That is what he observes and takes note of. And the only people remaining were those people who were citizens of that newly recognised country, as you yourself say. So why would they then withdraw to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia if they were in this newly recognised country? The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia cannot withdraw and pull out citizens of a neighbouring state, can it, withdraw it to its own territory? And Ghali here confirms the fact that Yugoslavia did fulfil its responsibilities and withdraw that portion of the JNA back to base, so to speak. And then he goes on to explain, if you have noted that, and I don't think that can be challenged or disputed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: After you note that, the witness should answer if he can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing that I can contribute with here would be to contrast Secretary-General Annan's review with the statement. I cannot -- I think that it would not be useful for me to comment on Boutros-Ghali's comment, report at that time which I just seen it for the first time today, even though I was a member of the Security Council at the time. But I can quote on Secretary-General Kofi Annan's precisely on that mission, precisely on this point, which it carries a completely different interpretation of what I've been hearing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Arria, you yourself mentioned a moment ago that it was because Yugoslavia did not carry out something it should have done that sanctions were imposed. And this is a report dated the 30th of May, 1992 and it states what I quoted. It also states clearly that the forces which remained in Bosnia beyond the control of the JNA. And then in point 10 it says the following: "As regards the withdrawal of the elements of the Croatian army [In English] [Previous translation continues]... now in Bosnia, information currently available in New York suggested no such withdrawal has occurred. UNPROFOR has received reliable reports of Croatian army personnel in uniform operating within and as part of military formation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Croatian authorities here consistently taken position that the Croatian soldiers in Bosnia and Herzegovina have left the Croatian army and are not subject to this authority. International observers do not, however, doubt that portions of Bosnia and Herzegovina are under control of Croatian military units, whether belonging to the local Territorial Defence, to paramilitary group, or to the Croatian army. It is unclear in the circumstances how their withdrawal or disbandment as required by the Council can be achieved." [Interpretation] Therefore -- therefore, three points. Ghali is saying three points here, that the JNA has withdrawn, that the army of Republika Srpska is outside any JNA control whatsoever, or the control of Belgrade in other words, and that the Croatian army has not withdrawn. And now I'm going to ask you, are you aware, Mr. Arria, of the fact that this report precisely was kept by the then-Chairman of the UN Security Council, Mr. Hohenfellner, the Austrian representative, that he did not divide it up among the UN Security Council members. He waited for the UN Security Council session to pass, at which sanctions against Yugoslavia were voted on, and he gave an explanation which is quite different from Ghali's report, and it was only after the sanctions had actually been enforced, introduced that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic -- Mr. Milosevic, stop. Mr. Milosevic, as a rule of thumb, no more than two or three sentences and then a question. Otherwise, it becomes very difficult for the witness and does not serve your interests also. It doesn't serve the interests of the trial. Let the witness answer now if he can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you can see, Your Honours, I was right. I never seen the report. It was not circulated. That is what has been said. But I can comment, make a general, very brief comment. That it was very convenient for Mr. Tudjman and for Mr. Milosevic to masquerade, to carry on a masquerade that these were local forces. These were forces coming from Croatia one time and coming from Belgrade. I don't think Mr. Mladic went to a military school in Pale. He went to military school, like all these officers, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Arria, it's very difficult for me to understand that this report of the Secretary-General was not circulated at that time. Are you positive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am positive. I have never seen this before. It's not the only time. As I said at the beginning, I have also seen other reports that have come to my attention 11 years later, and I have consulted with some of my colleagues at the time, and I -- if you read, Your Honour, in the French commission that evaluated, there are many gaps into the same thing because some of them didn't even know that these documents were circulated. That's why I alluded to a cover-up operation at the beginning where there were very few people who were not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does it have a Security Council number, the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It is a report -- yes, it has a number. It could be a general distribution document. It -- the Security Council number, as you -- I cannot compete now with your knowledge of the Security Council Resolution, always have a number, and it's SC, X number, et cetera, and they put the number and the date. This is not the case here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. But this is a report of the Secretary-General pursuant to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pursuant to. But I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But it would still have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It looks like a report. There's no doubt in my mind. You are absolutely correct, it looks like a report, but I have never seen it. I'm sorry, Your Honour, not to be able to provide more information now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the hour and 20 minutes will end in three minutes. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in response to that, Mr. Robinson, I ask you to extend my time for at least one hour, for one hour at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think one hour may be too much, but I'll consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. You will have the rest of this session, that is up to 12.30, and then ten minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson. I will try, then, to make a selection, but do bear in mind that I received a 500-paragraph long statement of this witness, and then it was shortened down only much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Arria, do you know that Peter Hohenfellner, who was president of the Security Council in the month of May 1992, that is to say at the time when this report of Ghali's was submitted to the Security Council for it to reach its further decisions on that -- on the basis of that report, that he kept this report, withheld it, waited for the session to end where sanctions were voted on, and this decision was based on facts which were totally not in line with the facts presented in the report? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know very well Ambassador Hohenfellner, and I know very well the Austrian people, and I cannot -- doubt that that would be the behaviour of Austria and of the ambassador, but that was -- it is really could be irrelevant, because the basis -- that would not alter or change at all the decision taken by the Security Council on sanction, not even by the closest people to Belgrade. It would not alter it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Arria. Isn't it obvious from the content of Ghali's report that he is not giving any basis for imposing sanctions on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Perhaps only against Croatia, because on one page he says that the JNA did withdraw but that the Croatian forces did not withdraw. And as you know full well, Austria was their ally, and now you say that Hohenfellner did not withhold the report although that is a material fact, because the report is dated the 30th of May. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any deceive by the Austria ambassador acting as president of the Security Council, Your Honour, and I haven't read the whole report, this report. You asked me to read a paragraph and I cannot speak for the whole document which I have not seen. I can speak to the paragraph that you had asked me to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Quite so, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to speed things up as much as I can, Mr. Robinson. I hope that that is quite clear, and I assume that this report of the Secretary-General has been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 444, when speaking about the negotiations in Geneva chaired by Owen and Stoltenberg, you say: "[In English]... when it came the moment to negotiate with the Muslim side, the negotiators agreed to bring seven members of the Presidency of that republic: Three Croatians, three Serbs, and one Muslim. I repeat, only one Muslim." [Interpretation] Quotation. Now, if we have the same Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in mind, I don't know which one you have in mind, it had a totality of seven members. Its ethnic composition could not have been determined by international negotiators. It had been established in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is not true at all that there was only one Muslim on the Presidency. Are you aware at least of that material fact, and also is that an indicator of the fact that you are using complete inaccuracies here? I've quoted you just now.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the time I said in a public meeting of the Security Council that the negotiator was trying to clinch a deal at any price, and then I said that it was bizarre to say the least that the negotiations in Geneva that could pull three of the other two parties, three members and one Muslim, and I said to the bad luck of the conveners that man was being searched by the police and had to leave the meeting, because he was the only one who were able -- that they were able to get to appear in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Never heard of any such thing, and I did not hear at all about any representative of the Muslim delegation, starting from Alija Izetbegovic onwards, he always had very numerous delegations, was mistreated by the police in Geneva or discriminated against. You are the first person to be claiming so. This is the first time that this has ever been heard.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only tell you that is in the record of my public statement. Lord Owen was there. It wasn't contested. The British representative was there. It wasn't contested. No one in the Security Council contested this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did this happen? Tell me, please. If you say that you have it in your notes, when was this meeting held when three Croats and three Serbs came from the Bosnian Presidency? Three Serbs were never on the Bosnian Presidency. There were two of them, Nikola Koljevic and Biljana Plavsic. I don't see how three could have come when they were not members of the Presidency at all.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not saying they were members of the Presidency. I said delegates. The three of the Croats, three of the Serbs, and one of the Muslims. I didn't say they were members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not dwell on this any longer. I believe that this is a completely unfounded allegation. In paragraph 11, which is highly unlikely for a witness, you put many questions. "[In English] Why did the UNSC delegate ex officio the main responsibility for the handling of the crisis to the EU (David Owen) and the United States (Cyrus Vance)?" [Interpretation] Now, tell me, you are putting this question. You are referring to the delegate of the European Union, David Owen, and the US envoy Cyrus Vance, and in the text further on you refer to Thorvald Stoltenberg who replaced Vance as UN envoy. It is obvious that you are aware of that fact because you referred to it. Stoltenberg is a Norwegian. That has nothing to do with the United States. So this question that you put, that they delegated people from the European Union and from the US, that's senseless, isn't it? Vance was elected or, rather, appointed and was there for a while and then he was succeeded by Stoltenberg. That's what you knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us what motivated the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it proved to be a major catastrophe, to say the least, for the poor Bosnians, that it was claimed that it was the hour of Europe and the European Community decided to assume responsibility, which they never discharged properly, and my question was raised more as a point to the international community. They -- I remember the Foreign Minister of Luxembourg, Mr. Poos, said this is the hour of Europe, it's not for the United Nations or the United Nations, this is our responsibility. And of course that responsibility was not discharged, and that's what I'm referring to. And what I add, Your Honour, was that the Security Council found that convenient, and it had to do it. Imagine this all happened in middle of Europe, that genocide was being committed and rape of women as a policy of a state was being committed in the middle of Europe after they had said 40 years before no more, never again. And this was happening again in the middle of Europe, that the Security Council didn't have any other option but to let the European Community to try to manage the issue. This is what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that there was a civil war going on over there and that atrocities or, rather, that in such a war and in such conflicts there could have been no parties involved who were innocent?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I restate my answer before: This was not civil war, this was a war of conquest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Milosevic, refrain from engaging in the question of the characterisation of the conflict, as I have told you before. That's a legal issue. So please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When speaking about the Security Council Resolution dated the 7th of February, 1992, and that is Resolution 740, in paragraph 60 you say: "[In English] When the Resolution was passed, I remember the satisfaction that the non-aligned members of the Council felt for having approved a Resolution to impose an arms embargo. Little did we know then that with that Resolution we were sealing the fate of the Bosnian republic, that we were taking away from this member country the right of self-defence enshrined in the UN Charter." [Interpretation] Tell me now, Mr. Arria, what kind of a member state are you talking about on the 7th of February, 1992? There was only one country then, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. At that time, Bosnia and Herzegovina had not even proclaimed its own independence, and it was recognised only on the 6th of April, 1992. And it was admitted into the UN on the 22nd of May in 1992. And you are talking about a Resolution dated the 7th of February. So that is to say three months before this which you call a member state of the UN had even existed as an internationally recognised state. And as you know, this unfortunate war was triggered by this premature recognition. Aren't you aware of that? Isn't that clear to you, Mr. Arria?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I am aware not only -- not only aware of the first part, but, Your Honours, that I said in my deposition that my country was a supporter preserving the integrity. It took very few weeks to find out under the conflict that Yugoslavia was not the Yugoslavia of Tito and that the accused was not just Josip Broz Tito either, and then that's when the position changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your last question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in paragraphs 53 through 56, you talk about your support to preserving the territorial integrity of the SFRY, and you refer to it just now. This same kind of support was given by other members of the non-aligned movement to Yugoslavia. Now, tell me, how is it that you can express regret, then, that the arming of secessionists was forbidden in the SFRY? Because according to the constitution of Yugoslavia, it was only the army and the Territorial Defence that had the right to be the armed force of Yugoslavia. For example, the Patriotic League of Bosnia-Herzegovina and other such organisations were illegal because they only pursued secession. Don't you know that? And had they been disarmed, there would have been no war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, will you please help me? Which is the question here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just rephrase the question briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that at that time there was support given to the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia? Isn't that right, Mr. Arria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In which date, Your Honour, I would like to ask Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The time before the recognition of these republics that had carried out secession. There was The Hague Conference, there were several statements by all sorts of world officials who supported the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Yugoslavia and so on. My question is, how can you express regret over the fact that the arming of secessionist political groups was being banned? That is to say they were trying to act apart from the constitution of Yugoslavia, and that was the only legitimate state, and they were trying to pursue violent secession.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the non-aligned movement in the United Nations kept the support of the integrity of the unity of Yugoslavia until Belgrade started shelling Croatia, and then it was clear that we were facing a war in the Balkans again. And what my remarks at that time was -- I'm referring to what happened, our knowledge of the situation in February 1992 that -- I'm commenting that had we known the intentions of Belgrade at the time, and we innocently thought that to put an arms embargo was actually like a great measure and a great help, and I said that this really meant that we left unarmed, and I believe, Your Honours, that's a major responsibility for the countries who knew this issue well, that they should be more accountable for having imposed and then later refusing in the -- even if confronting the realities on the ground, refused to lift the arms embargo which actually almost sealed the fate -- the fatal fate of the Bosnian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's time for the adjournment. We break for lunch and resume at 2.00 p.m. I remind you, Mr. Arria, during the adjournment you're not to discuss the case with anyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, ten minutes, to be applied strictly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. All right. I will really try to deal with two topics very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Arria, in paragraph 49 of the mission report to the Security Council established according to Resolution 819, "[In English] General Morillon and UNPROFOR military and civilian staff, et cetera ..." [Interpretation] So in April 1993, after visiting Bosnia-Herzegovina, you admired the generals and other members of UNPROFOR. And now you claim that they made the Muslim side surrender on the basis of the demilitarisation agreement. Is this a change in your position yet again?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am on the record for being an admirer of the efforts of the countries that put up the forces of UNPROFOR. Actually, that's one of paragraphs in the statement. I have actually even added that the government of Holland, the Netherlands, took an unfairly heavy load of responsibility upon themselves on the massacre at Srebrenica which should have set a precedent for the other countries to be more accountable, like the Dutch government, that even one government failed fell. I have never changed my opinion about UNPROFOR forces. When I said they were forced to capitulate and we understood at the moment it was because they knew on the ground that no other help, no other assistance was coming. Even Lord Owen had said before to President Izetbegovic, no one is coming to your assistance. So there was no other option at the moment for UNPROFOR forces but to do what they did. And I -- we said that in the report. It was not only my belief, it was the belief of all the members of the Security Council delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Arria. Do you know that this zone was not demilitarised, that the 28th Division was operating within it under the command of Naser Oric and that before these events in 1993 and after that the safe area was used as a support for committing terrible atrocities against the Serb villages around Srebrenica and around the area, that hundreds of people were killed and villages destroyed? Do you know anything about any of this?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: What I said at the moment, and I continue saying today, is that we knew that Srebrenica was surrounded, under siege, under siege, that it was being bombarded, shelled to the defenceless population. That is as much as we knew, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And did you know how much we from Serbia and I personally made an effort precisely in that year, 1993, in order to prevent larger-scale conflicts and these horrible consequences? At that time, it was supported by the leadership of Republika Srpska too in order to attain an agreement and to have an alleviation of the situation on the ground and that terrible atrocities were committed, horrific crimes. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I am aware, Your Honour, that Mr. Milosevic stated through a long period of time all kinds of promises and statements that were not fulfilled until international community took a firm action and stopped him. That's as much as we all know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any promises that I gave, promises that I gave and did not fulfil, but we don't have time to go into that now. And now this other issue I wish to deal with. It seems to me that your most telling proof of what you have been saying, that Serbs committed genocide and that Yugoslavia committed genocide against the Muslims, and you keep referring to the 8th of April, 1993, ruling of the International Court on provisional measures. Isn't that right, Mr. Arria?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's very important that I clear -- I have never addressed the Yugoslavian people as a whole, for whom I have great admiration. They are not to be blamed for the faults and crimes committed under the name of their country. It's terrible what has been brought also to the Serbian population because of the practices promoted and implemented by the Belgrade regime, never addressed them as Yugoslavian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Arria, I'm not asking you about whether you spoke about that. You say that the International Court of Justice, by their measures taken on the 8th of April, 1993, in connection with the Convention on Genocide, Bosnia-Herzegovina brought charges against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In paragraphs 178 and 180, you say: "[In English] The following provisional measures to be in effect while the court is seized of this case." 179: "That Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) together with its agents and surrogates in Bosnia and elsewhere must immediately cease and desist from all acts of genocide and genocidal acts against the people and the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina including but not limited to murder, summary executions, torture, rape, mayhem, so-called ethnic cleansing, the wanton devastation of villages, towns, districts and cities, the seige of villages, towns, the starvation of the civilian population, the bombardment of civilian population centres and the detention of civilians in concentration camps." [Interpretation] That is what you said the position of the International Court of Justice was. However, my question to you, Mr. Arria, is the following: Isn't it clear to you from the actual text that you've quoted from that what you say is not an integral part of the decision of the ICJ at all? This sentence is part of the request put forth by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is not part of the court ruling. So you, Mr. Arria, deceive those who are listening to this, claiming that what I just quoted to you now is part of the court ruling, the court order, and you actually quoted the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And of course, their document is worded in the worst possible way against the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was the first time ever the International Court of Justice took a case such as this and took it on the monumental evidence provided to it. This is only one part, one quote from the whole court order by the International Court of Justice. If we take a minute to read the other parts of the court order, you will see that that's repeated throughout the whole document. This is the most detailed court order because it was the first time ever that the issue of genocide was being considered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I understand Mr. Milosevic to be saying is that what is in paragraph 179 reflects the request made for provisional measures and does not itself form a part of the actual decision. One would need to look at the judgement itself to be sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you know full well, and I hope that Mr. Arria, with his diplomatic experience, would have to know that when provisional measures are taken by the International Court of Justice, they do not go into the merit of the case, and they do not establish the factual basis. They just remind that there is the duty to abide by the provisions of the convention, but they do not rule that there actually had been a violation of them. Please look at this document. I got it in your tab number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So after all of this, and of course there are quotations of sentences provided by the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because after all that is what they are ruling on, after all those quotations, it says very nicely on page 24: "[In English] For these reasons the court indicates, pending its final decision in the proceedings instituted on 20th of March 1993 by Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the following provisional measures: A, the government of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia should immediately in pursuance of its undertaking in the Convention of the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide on 9 December 1948 take all measures within its power to prevent commission of the crime of genocide." [Interpretation] And paragraph 2: "[In English] Yugoslavia should in particular ensure that military, paramilitary, or irregular armed units which may be," [Interpretation] would like to emphasise may be, "as any organisation and person which may be subject to its control, direction or influence do not commit any act of genocide or conspiracy to commit genocide of direct and public instrument to commit genocide or of complicity in genocide whether directed against the Muslim population of Bosnia-Herzegovina or against any other national, ethnic, racial or religious group." [Interpretation] And finally under B: "[In English] The Yugoslavian government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina should not take any action and should ensure that no action is taken which may aggravate or extend the existing dispute over the prevention of punishment of crime of genocide or render it more difficult a solution."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic, stop. We have the ICJ decision, and we can look at it to see what it actually says. It appears, however, that what is in paragraph 180 of the statement, the witness's statement, is reflected in the second paragraph on page 24 of the decision, but what is in paragraph 179 of the statement does not appear to be reflected. But we have the decision, as I said, and we can -- we'll have a look at it, and we'll make up our own minds. So please proceed. In any event, you are beyond the ten minutes now. So I think you have to stop. The amicus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dr. Arria, I've got some questions which essentially deal with the report that you made for the United Nations and deal with the comments you made in various press conferences. So if you could turn, first of all, to tab 17 of our exhibit file.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 17, and it's headed "Transcriptions from Arria tapes." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you'll see within this section apparently a number of recorded statements that were made by you and others after you had visited Srebrenica and during your visit to the region and the statements that were made there. And if we could look first of all at that first page, at the foot of it, and there's a paragraph that begins: "No, these conditions have not been known. This is the first time. I am a member of the Security Council. My colleagues never knew this. We have to ask permission for a doctor to enter Srebrenica," and it goes on to say you're really shocked and it's a serious matter, and you were shocked to see the conditions. Now, the issue in your evidence concerns notice and knowledge, and what it seems to be saying here, which may be slightly different from your testimony earlier today, that you did not know about the conditions within Srebrenica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. The situation and conditions as I describe them in this press statement which were made to BBC of London, which gave me a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you comment on page 2, if we look at the second paragraph, saying what the UN authorities have done there is extraordinary, and you refer to particular troops from countries such as Canada, Bangladesh, Russia, and Denmark. So it seems you were impressed by what the UN authorities had done within Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. I stated that previously. I never ceased my admiration for the men and women who served under UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to the next page, which is headed in the top right-hand corner "842" as the numbering, and we see paragraphs there. If we turn to the fourth -- or third paragraph, second to last sentence. You refer to the UNHCR doing a wonderful job. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "We absolutely should help those who are not residents and want to leave." And in the next paragraph you mention: "We met with the Muslim government, and they did not express that they did not wish their people to leave. No one in the streets approaches us to ask if they want to leave." Was there an issue then that in fact people within that safe haven, that the civil authorities wanted to keep a large number of civilian people within Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: That was not our impression at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there an issue that people were not saying that they wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: We would have been surprised people didn't want to leave, living suffering under those conditions. Actually, we were impressed by the opposite, that they didn't want to leave, living under those extreme circumstances, under siege and surrounded by the Serb paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
