utterances.text: Yes. Srebrenica was a community of a certain size. The figure escapes me, you might be able to correct me, but I think 10.000 population that had become the home to 40.000 plus people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: There were 70.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Seventy thousand. You correct me. So the whole population in this place had expanded to a degree that the actual community there didn't have the facilities and structure to cope with that number of refugees.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It didn't even satisfy the conditions for 500 people, even less, of course. By the time we got there, there weren't 70.000. There were around 10.000 to 15.000 when we got to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the point is that this safe haven was created importing a large number of people beyond the level to which that particular town could deal with those numbers. It was simply not equipped to deal with those numbers.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: This is first time I hear that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, isn't that why there was horrific conditions concerning water, concerning the way people were living? There was insufficient housing, there was insufficient food. This place had not been established to cope with that number of people.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The reality was completely opposite, sir. There were no houses because they had been shelled. There were no houses because they had been destroyed. There were no medicines, there was no water because it had been cut. There was no electricity because it had been cut. Even 500 people could not live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were you aware at the time that you were there that in fact there was an issue that was being put forward by the Bosnian Serbs that they were facing attacks from Muslim forces who were kept within that enclave?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: You know, I had company, sir, the Canadian Battalion commander in Srebrenica, and you will see -- I have never forgotten that Brigadier Hayes introduced me to the Serb officers by name - this is Colonel Such-and-such, Major Such-and-such - and then he looked at the ones on the right who were almost dressed like civilians and said these are also my friends on the Muslim side. They were very lightly armed and you would have to be blind not to see that the town was surrounded by heavy weapons and very heavy artillery and under the absolute control of the Serb paramilitary forces, and the kinds of armament actually UNPROFOR found later on, they were very light weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That may have been the case about the armory that was surrounding Srebrenica. I'm not asking about that. I'm asking whether you were aware of the issue that there were forces led by a commander going out from Srebrenica who were fighting the Bosnian Serb forces in the surrounding territory. Were you aware of that as an issue?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: That was an issue that was always raised by Mr. Karadzic. That I absolutely recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were you aware of the name of the commander who was said to be of those particular forces, a man called Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we just turn over to the next page, then, the -- if we turn over to the next page, then, the figures end in 843. And it's in the middle of the large -- there's a large paragraph in the middle of the page. One of your UNHCR representatives had explained that the town is overcrowded, it's impossible to assist all the population, problems for doctors, materials, foods, every day comforts. And in the middle of the page there is this: "But the main question is should we fight for the right of the people to be evacuated from Srebrenica or for the right to stay in dignity and safety? The UNHCR here will do whatever we can, and I hope that the politicians and ambassadors will help us in negotiating expansion of the safe area." So firstly, going back to that issue, people did not -- or people were being subject to a decision made by the civilian authorities within Srebrenica, telling them not to leave the safe haven. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: We created -- we thought that we passed a Resolution, Your Honours, to create a safe area, and of course it was far away from. It was a very unsafe area. So much so that when we returned to New York, we said to the Security Council we cannot repeat this experience in the next safe areas which were recommended, for those cities, and eventually, as Your Honours remember, there was another very unsafe area Resolution which did not prevent the repetition of the experiences that were suffered by the people in Srebrenica. That's how I recall these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Moving back to your report, then, which is in tab 15, and I'm looking at what has in the top left-hand corner page 4.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It's not my report, Your Honour. It's the report of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry. You're just the vehicle in court and I appreciate it was others, but it's come to be known -- it's come to be identified with you. So if we look at the report that you were a party to making, page 4 sets out the mandate and scope of activities, and you list in paragraph 3 the leaders of the three parties to the conflict whom you met. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic, Dr. Karadzic, and Mate Boban. You didn't meet Mr. -- President Milosevic on this -- during this report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You conducted interviews. You have said several remarks during the course of your evidence about the various parties, but it's correct that it was reported to you that all sides were committing atrocities at different levels but only the Serbs are taking territory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I was informed of that. I was also informed what the Secretary-General Kofi Annan called at the time the moral equivalence of the parties as completely different in importance and significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that is why you were seeing all the parties to the conflict, from the Croat leadership to the Bosnian Serb leadership to the Bosnian Muslim leadership, because you were aware that this conflict involved three parties.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Not completely like that, sir. We did not see at the time President Milosevic for one reason specifically, because we did not want to interfere in the negotiations that were being under going in the Lord Owen and Secretary Vance. That was exactly the reason why we didn't include him in our agenda. Not because we thought that he was not a party. On the contrary. We thought he was the main party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But it seems, though, that from -- you don't mention that within this report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, I think I mention it in the report, why we didn't meet with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: And if you want, I'll read it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could point it out to me and let me know where it is.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I'll have to take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In fact, the Judges can probably look at that in their own time and it can be re-examined on if it's there, Dr. Arria. My time is very brief, as you will understand, and that is why I'm dealing with one issue and trying to deal with it as rapidly as possible. If we go to page 7 of the report, at the foot of the page, paragraph 27(C), Dr. Karadzic indicated to the mission at its meeting with him at the Belgrade airport that he would not take the town, that the water supply would be immediately restored and that humanitarian convoys would be allowed. It would be right to say that in terms of forces at that stage, it was obvious that Dr. Karadzic had sufficient troops and weaponry, if he had wanted to, to have gone into Srebrenica there and then.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, actually he was not telling the truth, and we express in the report. He had already taken the town. The town was an open gaol. And actually, when we entered into Srebrenica, I went in the United Nations armoured car, and the car behind me was the head of the Serb paramilitary, Colonel Ratko, parading around town with Brigadier General Hayes. If that's not a sign of control of the town, I wouldn't know what else could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But it's a world apart from actually being in the town and having taken over its government, infrastructure, and having troops on the streets, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: There was no infrastructure, there were no troops on the street. There was only poor people couldn't have a house, couldn't have water, couldn't have doctors, couldn't have medicines. There were epidemics around. So it was easier to leave the poor people in the village to take care of themselves. It was an open gaol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This was a matter that was known about by you, then, and others, presumably, on your mission for the United Nations, of Dr. Karadzic's ability at this time in 1993, the position that he was in?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Which position, if you can tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of having surrounded and made Srebrenica an open gaol, as you've described it.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: We actually described it to him, because he acted like he didn't know. And he of course promised that the water would be resumed and the doctors be allowed into town, and the tents be allowed into town, which he never did, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. But having seen Srebrenica, if we look at your observations within page 11 and the two paragraphs that have been dealt with so far, paragraphs 46 and 47, in fact, the position that you and your mission had come to was that the safe haven should remain. The mandate may be changed as far as UNPROFOR was concerned, but that the use of a -- a place such as Srebrenica should be maintained.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I'm not following the last part of your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All right. Isn't that right? That is the position. If we look at 47, the mission recognises, and that is the creation that enclaves are safe areas deserving serious consideration, as you say in paragraph 46, but a larger UNPROFOR presence, a revised mandate to accompany cease-fire and safe area monitoring and different rules of engagement but stopping short of a military strike enforcement.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I don't understand. Is that a question or are you quoting my statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am quoting your statement and I am putting to you --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I stand behind that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So that is the position you had found yourself in rather than tearing up the rule book as far as Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Sorry, what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tearing up the rule book. Rather than changing the whole policy concerning Srebrenica, you had decided with your mission that that policy should be continued.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No. On the contrary. When we came back to New York, one of the points in the report says that the bad experience of Srebrenica should not be repeated and we recommended the creation of other safe areas based on different terms. It's the opposite of what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps there's a misunderstanding between you and me on that issue, but I'll leave the matter there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, just to return to a question that you asked earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were you asking the witness whether the conditions in Srebrenica, the suffering of the Muslims was due primarily or only to overcrowding in contradistinction to anything else, any other cause?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- if we turn to that particular section of the press conference. Tab 17. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was being said at the time was the damage to the particular town, including damage to the school, damage to the buildings, but that the circumstances in which the people were living was also due to the numbers, the sheer numbers of people who were taking refuge within the particular confines of that place. At the top of page 843 is the remark that the town is so overcrowded it's impossible to assist all the population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you like me to comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may comment on that paragraph, clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. You know, that would be a major recreation of the circumstances. Your Honour, I visit the school, one of the schools in Srebrenica where five days before we arrived, or a week before we arrived, the same Serbian colonel who was accompanying us had shelled the city of Srebrenica and there were still remains of children on the patio. With a city without doctors, without medicines. I admit it must be true that many people came afterwards, because the small villages around Srebrenica had already been run over by the Serb paramilitary, but by no measure of the imagination it's possible to conceive that people could live under those circumstances, no water, no electricity, no surgeon, no houses. People were living on the streets, Your Honour. When we talk about infrastructure, there was no infrastructure to talk about. And on top of that, they were surrounded, intimidated by the pressure of very heavy armed people, and the people knew already that the United Nations didn't have any control. I don't think what happened was so much -- public opinion was concentrated those days on the enclave that nothing more could happen. I think that was our contribution at the time. As time passed by, Srebrenica ceased to be in the centre of attention of the world opinion, and as we all know, we all know how this sad chapter for humanity ends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One or two points to pick up on, please, Mr. Arria.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On tab 15, the report, you've been asked about these paragraphs 46 and 47, it being suggested that you were in favour of continuation or enlargement of the safe area policy. Your recommendation, was it for more of the same or was it for something totally different?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Something totally different. The only thing it had in common was the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the differences that you regarded as essential if the interests of the citizens were to be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What were the differences? What --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The differences is we had asked for protection. This is one thing, Your Honour, it is interesting to note. I'm sure know about it, in the United Nations, in the drafting the language, semantics plays a very important role. In French version it was "la protection," in Spanish it was "ellos protohijos [phoen]," and in English it was "safe areas," and each one chose his own interpretation. And this is what happened. Not only in that, I cannot really imagine how many other documents of the Security Council the same thing goes and happens but with a mandate for something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've referred to it, indeed your report or your -- your, as you describe it, affidavit speaks of the moral equivalence spoken of by Mr. Annan. Can you just explain that term and its significance.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The UN had a tradition, a custom to apply this term both parties, aggressors and victims, like they were on the same. And I think Secretary-General Kofi Annan called it the moral equivalence of the parties to put the perpetrators and the victims in the same consideration was like to appear to be neutral in something which was difficult to be neutral.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But was neutrality being represented here --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- in a moral equivalence or was there some lack of neutrality --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It could be a combination, but it was also a reaction not to be more involved than they should -- they wanted to be. That's one of the reasons I said this morning the Council of Genocide. There was so much effort to even get that into a Resolution, even though it was coming from the International Court of Justice, because the Convention on Prevention of Genocide should have obligated the parties to do something about it. So to acknowledge this was taking place would have put them in a very difficult situation, and that's why many of the permanent members decided that it wasn't a good idea to be so forceful on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the -- were the armies that hadn't been recognised, the Republika Srpska army and so on, treated in the same or a different way for purposes of equivalence to the state itself?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I'm not understanding you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I haven't asked the question well. I may come back to it but let's move on. By the way, your reference to not meeting Milosevic is in your affidavit at paragraph 301. It may not be in the report. I think that may be what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Thank you. I know I said it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said that Karadzic complained of Muslim forces attacking out of Srebrenica. When you were there, you were in the presence of the Serb soldiers who appeared to be confident and in charge; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they complain to you, the ones actually on the ground, did they complain to you in the way that Mr. Kay's been raising, of any attackings coming from out of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Not at all. They were even walking around the city unarmed or maybe they had a pistol. The colonel marched into Belgrade United Nations force never expressed any concern at all about troops of Bosnians in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Mr. Kay asked you two other questions for which I have follow-ups. One is you were giving a general account of the lack of water, lack of medicines. Can you just give us one example, I think it's in your report, about the water and Karadzic. Did he deal with that, turning it on or off?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: We had the meeting, Dr. Karadzic at the airport, he was just coming to visit Mr. Milosevic in his office. That was the we met in Belgrade, because that's where he used to dispatch very often. And when we met him at the airport of Belgrade, I told him General Dr. Karadzic the water problem is something that can be solved immediately, and he said I will solve this immediately. He never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally from Mr. Kay's questions, you speak of your admiration for the UNPROFOR forces but you've also spoken of the way in which the forces you saw were subordinate to the Serb forces. That's the Canadian Forces, I think, at the time.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No. This situation was with the British officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: British officers.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: This was not actually in Srebrenica. I think on the contrary. The Canadian Battalion commander was extremely angry at the lack of support he had. And not only -- and also many British officials privately complained to me of the orders that they had to perform, like do not rock the boat. That was the general policy. Do not create too many problems. Do not get us involved. So that was the reason they had those, I would say subservient -- acting in relationship with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So your admiration for the forces takes account of the fact that they were acting in the way they did and for the reasons you've given?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, and acting under instructions, of course, the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the ICJ case, Your Honour, and the references to that, I think I dealt in the few questions in examination-in-chief with the distinction between the recital and the conclusions. Yes. I think I've asked that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's been really suggested to you by the accused that you were taken in by the public relations of, for example, Bosnia. You were deceived by it because it was a propaganda war. Just remind us in short form how, if at all, you thought you were able to achieve balanced reporting, how you got enough information to have a balanced view.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The only fact that convinced us, Your Honours, what was happening was the reality on the ground. I don't think any propaganda war, I never met any of the lobbyists, of the Bosnians. The issue here, when I became member of the Security Council I didn't think I was representing only my country. I was representing the region as a whole. And I vowed not to be a bystander, and I would -- and that's the reason why I'm here, because I was not a bystander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were very concerned to go on this mission to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: We wanted to see what was happening because we were by that time receiving all kinds of information. The president of the Security Council was a Pakistan ambassador at that time, Marker. It was not easy to get the mission to be approved to be sent to Srebrenica. It was a long discussion for about two hours at night in the Security Council. Then they appointed me to head the mission, to really, you know, gather the facts on the ground, and it was a very important visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what you saw, as the accused has suggested was propaganda war, did this fit in with the general reporting that you were getting from the press and the media or did it change your view, or did it confirm your view? Just explain.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It was worse. Your Honour, I mentioned this morning that a British journalist was the first one who showed the world what was happening, and that prompted General Morillon and prompted the Security Council to act, but when we got there, it was much worse. It was unimaginable. I remember telling the Russian Ambassador who had -- who was in a position to our policy at the Security Council. I said you always talk of Leningrad. There is another Leningrad in a different scale. You have to see it on your own. And even the Russian ambassador who was with us on the mission shared this in our report. He signed the report which was a consensus report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two last questions. You've been asked by the accused about what he said in a particular report about ethnic cleansing being a criminal act. You told us of what you regarded as the accused's two-prong approach. You remember. Does his being reported as saying that ethnic cleansing was a criminal act fit in with your understanding of the two-pronged approach?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. You know, I remember explaining to the members of Security Council. I said we finally understood the full meaning of ethnic cleansing. Ethnic cleansing is putting bombs under the roofs of the homes, it's to intimidate, to terrorise and to eliminate the possessions and to move them and to displace them. That's ethnic cleansing. I said now we don't have to read it, now we know what it means. It was the first time that we really could grasp the meaning of this terrible policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood my question. It was my mistake. Did the accused's saying publicly that ethnic cleansing was a crime fit with your description of his having a two-pronged approach?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Absolutely. You know, it was very clear to us that it was, like you said, a two-pronged approach; one from Belgrade entertaining the international community in endless negotiation, paramilitary negotiation. On the other side I said this morning the proxies, Mladic, Karadzic and others in Bosnia-Herzegovina, executing the policy of ethnic cleansing, genocide, crimes against humanity. So it was until the moment came when these two-prong approach was stopped by the international community, but this served to conquer more territory and to change the geography of a sovereign state of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that brings me indeed, by the phrase "change the geography," to my last question. The phrase "Greater Serbia" suggested as, I think, a fiction by the accused has been used by you in your report, not associating it with necessarily the speech of the accused himself. But your understanding at the time of Greater Serbia or the intention to create a Greater Serbia was what?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It was understood there was not one media or one report that didn't speak of the Greater Serbia. It would be difficult to understand how a country in the former Republic of Yugoslavia was willing to accept these sanctions imposed upon them if they have anything to gain in this process, and the thing to gain was a larger territory controlled by proxies in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No other questions of this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, just a minute, please. Since Mr. Nice mentioned only now the meeting with Karadzic at the airport, just one question. Just one question for the witness please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Arria, since you met Karadzic on the 26th of April at the airport, as you said here, the Belgrade airport, and he said to you that he had been at a meeting with me, the question is, do you know that only a few days later in Athens, on the 1st of May, a peace conference was held under the auspices of the Greek Premier, Constantin Mitsotakis, where Vance and Owen presented their plan and at that conference Karadzic signed the Vance-Owen Peace Plan? So it was a few days after that meeting. Do you remember that or not?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the meeting in Athens, which I even quote in my official speeches in the Security Council, the negotiators allow something which we thought and I stated officially was uncalled for. This is true Mr. Karadzic signed, but with the proviso that he will have to get the authorisation and confirmation from a so-called congress or parliament in the so-called Republika Srpska, which didn't exist, and the negotiations allowed that to happen. And Your Honour, if I may add, like, I have another question, on the disappearance of this mysterious document that you asked me this morning of Secretary-General Boutros-Ghali, the only way -- you remember Mr. Milosevic asked me do you know, have you seen this document? I said no. He said this document was circulated to the Security Council. After I said, no, it wasn't, then he said, well, this document was retained by the Austrian Ambassador, who was the president of the Security Council, who wanted to impose sanctions and hid it from the Security Council. The only way that this could have happened was Mr. Boutros-Ghali to be in connivance with him in complicity, and that was not the case. I cannot imagine Mr. Boutros-Ghali allowing the Austrian ambassador to hide a report from him addressed to the Security Council. I just wanted to add that as a contribution to the point you made this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Arria.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the next witness who is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before you proceed, I want to deal with two matters raised by Mr. Milosevic this morning. The first one is a follow-up to the order made by the Chamber that the Registrar would give him as much assistance as it could during this phase of the case, and he said he had not received any. I have caused inquiries to be made, and I am to say that Mr. Milosevic, you are to raise this matter with the Registrar, let him know what assistance you need, and he will, to the extent that he can, provide the assistance. In particular, if you need more time for consultations with your associates, that's the kind of assistance that he would be in a position to grant. The second matter raised by Mr. Milosevic had to do with the effect of the decision of the Registrar on communication. Mr. Milosevic maintained that the effect of that decision would be that he would be hampered in the preparation of his case. I've looked at the decision itself, Mr. Milosevic, and it explicitly states that the restrictions do not apply to communications and visits reasonably necessary for the preparation of your case, including interviewing by telephone or in person potential witnesses or otherwise collecting evidence in his defence provided that the facility is not to be used in any manner for any contacts with the media. So your right to prepare your case is not prejudiced in any way by the decision. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we turn from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apologies. Before we turn from the last witness, he was, in the course of cross-examination, asked a large number of questions of a detailed nature about his statement. I'm entirely in the Court's hands. It might be more convenient for the statement to be exhibited principally for reference to the passages to which Mr. -- the accused referred but generally where there's extensive cross-examination on grounds of credibility or reliability on a witness's statement, it may be thought appropriate to exhibit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you have any comments on that, exhibiting the statement of the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- of the last witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Mr. Robinson. That statement contains 500 paragraphs, and as you know full well, I did not have the opportunity of dealing with more than one fifth of it. I mean, I could not deal with four-fifths because of the time limit that was imposed and because of the evasiveness of this statement. It is no doubt evasive and not relevant. This story looks like a newspaper article to me more than anything else. It is supposed to support this false indictment and it doesn't really prove a thing. It just shows what the witness's line of thinking is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I see you're getting ready to rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I could just assist the Court. The Court passed an order as to the confines of the statement. That statement well and truly exceeds that. It is also full of opinion and observations and personal opinions of that particular witness. In my submission, the extent of that statement does not require, as a result of the cross-examination, the evidence heard live in court, for it to be made an exhibit as a result of what the Court heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The decision is not to admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases. Before the next witness, there's one administrative matter to be dealt with, and after the next break I suspect I will have to come to the question of the order of witnesses for tomorrow. I'm not in a position finally to come to it at the moment. So may I deal with the first administrative problem now, which can be dealt with in open court, bearing in mind that the next witness is protected to some degree. With the change of the timetable, there is no date within the current schedule on which Mr. Bildt can come. He was originally coming, I think, last week on the 4th, and I've explored with him his diary for this week; today, tomorrow, and Thursday the 12th; next week the 18th and 19th. Without going into it in any great detail, he is between several -- well, two or three continents, I'm not quite sure how many, in that one-week period, returning to Northern Europe, he would be available on the afternoons of either this Friday, next Monday, or next Tuesday, but he is completely unavailable for the other remaining four days. He was a witness who, as the Chamber will recall, we sought to add both because he can provide valuable evidence over a short time period but also because, in our submission, it's evidence that will give a context or deepen the context of other evidence that's very important for the Chamber to assess in relation to the accused's state of knowledge and activities at the time of the Srebrenica massacre, and it was for that evidence that we sought leave to add him to the list. Of course he could give a great deal of other evidence because of his position, but that wasn't critical to our application, and we would still not be seeking to lead any evidence of it, although the Chamber was comparatively generous in the cross-examination allowed so that, overall, his evidence could last three hours, perhaps a little longer. I don't obviously seek an immediate response, but I would ask the Chamber to consider adjusting the timetable so that he might give evidence, perhaps next week, given that his inability to come on the day fixed for him was not as a result of any action of his or ours but through forces outside our control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We hear the submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next witness is entitled to protection by your order. May I respectfully suggest that we go briefly into closed session for the opening parts of his testimony and for consideration of how to deal with his evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- read out literally the topics covered by the witness in his statements, picking up at the exhibits and informing Your Honours where those exhibits have already been tendered so that you can mark your papers accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness B-1804, in your first statement -- just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your first statement, did you deal with the withdrawal and deployment of your then-unit to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, I did answer those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You went on to deal with the conditions in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And to deal with the takeover of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I was asked several questions in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will see that tab 2 in the bundle is a document that relates to paragraph 24. We take the view on review and in order to save burdening the Chamber that it's an exhibit that we needn't bother with so it need not be produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me clarify this. What are included in tab 1, the two statements --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No just the first statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first statement, together with the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we strike tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You then went on, Witness B-1804, to deal with the arming of Serbs in Zvornik, and at paragraph 33 dealt with a document called the Variant A and B document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will see this is in your papers at tab 3. It has previously been exhibited, and therefore, subject to how the Court orders its papers, need not become a burden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You went on to deal with the attack on Zvornik, with Kula Grad, with the cleansing, as described, of Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And at paragraph 52, in that section, you deal with an exhibit again previously tendered, the decision on strategic objectives of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You turned to the creation of the VRS and then dealt with Srebrenica, focusing first on the relationship between the VRS and the JNA, or VJ, including the 30th Personnel Centre, and at paragraph 72 dealt with an intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, intercepts are, save perhaps with one exception or maybe more than one, but the exception being dealt with by being marked for identification only in the conduct of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this particular intercept you dealt with as a document confirming payment of salaries from Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: One detail slightly outside the statement but just for the avoidance of doubt: When you were paid, you yourself were paid money, as you explain, from Belgrade right the way through the period we are concerned with, you were paid at the rank appropriate -- at the rate appropriate to your rank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that relates to the entire period with which your two statements are concerned.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. Just an interruption of five or six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not a question of when paid from Belgrade simply getting a reduced amount of money constituting social security, you were paid the rate appropriate to your rank in the services.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 6 you dealt with in the section of your statement follows, following support from the VJ to the VRS and with examples, and this was an intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point may we perhaps go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: With -- in the next section on the planning of the proposed attack on Srebrenica, tab 8, a document you were able to produce or identify, although it's been previously exhibited, and that was a command of the Drina Corps of the 2nd of July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I have had a look at that document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You dealt with the objective of the attack, with the expectations prior to the attack on the Srebrenica area, and at paragraph 111 within this section, you produced or you identified an exhibit already produced, tab 9, a directive for further operations issued by the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Already produced, Your Honours, as you will see, 553, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You dealt with the embargo imposed on Republika Srpska, with the lack of direct VJ involvement in the military attack on Srebrenica safe area, saying that so far as you were aware, no VJ units or personnel took part in any direct combat action in the 1995 military operation to attack and -- the Srebrenica safe area?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After the fall of Srebrenica was the next section of your first statement, and then in the section dealing with General Krstic at tab 10, may we look at that, please? At paragraph 125, you see an identification card of Krstic, the rank of major general from Belgrade, and of course a VJ military service and identification card; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At tab 11 in the same section but at your paragraph 131, a further identification card to the same general effect, and you can authenticate it; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: This is the civilian identification card.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At tabs 12 to 17, Your Honours will see have already been produced or tendered, and -- Your Honour, I think we must now return to private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- being an organigramme of the Main Staff VRS structure, which you were able to confirm as accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with certain remarks that I made on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in the following tab, tab 19, there's another organigramme of the Main Staff of the VRS. Again you were an able to confirm the data at least in part?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. There were two organigrammes, one of the Main Staff and the second of the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The following tab, tab 20, gives VRS code names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if Your Honours have this before you, I think the witness can take us down, as he says in paragraph 144, to Domar, that he doesn't know the call-signs after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 146 produces tab 21, an order dated the 8th of April of 1994, which lists, at page 6, Gojko Simic as a member of the Zvornik Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. I was shown an order by the brigade commander where that name was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At tab 22, paragraph 107 -- 147 is a document perhaps you could just look at, please. Does this appear to you to be a genuine document?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: This is a copy of the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Signed by Pandurevic. And on page 3 in the English, under the Organ for Combat Arms, we can see Maksimovic and Kajtaz as on the records for the General Staff of the VJ; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I apologise, but may I just take a minute to find that? Yes. I found it under number 8 and 9, the organ for the services for the brigade. Maksimovic Milos Captain First Class and Kajtaz Milenko Captain First Class. They weren't in the masons staff but in the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As we turn to page 21 of the witness's statement, the Chamber should know that from the top of the page of the English version, two lines have been inadvertently missed out and we've got a substitute page that I hope is before you that provides those two missing lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's page 20 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 23, actually, is dealt with in that paragraph that we're looking at and is a document that the witness is able to identify, although a copy, as he correctly says, as being an identical one -- original one properly copied coming from Zivanovic, a major general of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tabs 24, 5, 6, and 7 deal with vehicle logs, and the Chamber will see, looking at tab 24, the dates in the second half of July 1995 at 24, and then it will see the logs of personnel of the logistics platoon company for tab 25. For tab 26 it will see the log of presence of personnel for the battalion. And for tab 27, the work of vehicle maintenance and generators, again with dates in July. And we then come to tab 28, dealt with at paragraph 154, which is the death certificate of Gojko Simic, which, Witness 1804, you were able to identify as, I think, an authenticate document.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. I have had a look at that document too, earlier on when you showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And finally tab 29, dealt with at paragraph 155, is a document that you looked at for the military police dealing with attendance roster for July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we then please go into private session for tab 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sets out matters at paragraph 1 to 3 which are background that I won't cover, sets out general areas of history for material matters in the following paragraphs, gives a chronology of material events in the middle of 1995 and then sets out in some detail some of the events that happened at the fall of Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will see what is, and I don't need to go into private session to deal with this -- perhaps -- no, perhaps I should to assist the Chamber. Can we go, sorry, into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before the cross-examination commences, I want to say that this witness is a protected witness. That means he's subject to certain protective measures, and protective measures are an important element in the administration of justice in this Tribunal. As such, any person breaching the protective measures will be subject to prosecution, and so I advise and warn the media and others that any reporting of the witness's testimony that tends to identify him would amount to a contempt of court and be punishable under Rule 77 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, tell me, how much time are you giving me for this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we had assigned two and a half hours, and it would be subject to the same thing that I said this morning; if you have an application to make, should you choose to use the entire time, you may make it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I will be able to assess that tomorrow, thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1804 --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were an active JNA officer; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, before any conflict broke out in the former Yugoslavia, although you hail from Bosnia-Herzegovina, you did your military service or, rather, no, not your military service but you were in the military outside Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that it was the usual practice, in view of the fact that the Yugoslav People's Army was multi-ethnic, that officers, depending on the requirements of the service, be assigned throughout Yugoslavia without any constraints in terms of the republic they originally came from?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the units that you served in, did you work as an officer together with members of all other ethnic groups in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Among you, were there any tensions in view of the fact that you belonged to different national or ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when did the first crises and tensions appear in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, sometime just before the war in Slovenia broke out, if I remember correctly. So perhaps -- let me say 1991, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You were withdrawn from the area where you had been serving. You were withdrawn to Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where other units were withdrawn to from your corps or from part of the army district that you had served in?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, I could not give an exact answer to your question in view of my position then, but they were withdrawn to Bosnia, Vojvodina, Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I will try to work as efficiently as possible so that we would make the best possible use of our time. So I'm going to start dealing with some matters that were brought up in your statement. In paragraph 11 of your statement, you say that the practice was in the JNA, when the conflicts started, that is, and that is what paragraph 11 of your statement pertains to, that paramilitary units were involved in combat activities, and you mentioned Seselj's men, Dragan's men, and others by way of an example here. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in that case would these units be under the command of the JNA or were they able to move about independently and to operate without any kind of superior command?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: On the basis of what I heard and what I know, these different paramilitary units took part in combat activities voluntarily if they wanted to take part in such activities. And when actual combat would take place, then they were operating on the basis of command. So within the combat operation itself under the command of the JNA officer in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of any order of a superior officer or any superior related to paramilitary units that were not willing to be under the command of the JNA, that such paramilitary units would have to be disbanded, disarmed, arrested, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I do not recall such an order, but I do remember that in Zvornik there was an intervention when the units of the Protection Regiment expelled a paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They expelled a paramilitary unit which was engaged in unlawful acts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat? Yes, he said Zuca. And this man Zuca was later arrested in Serbia. I assume you know that. And tell me, please, these combat activities which took place in Croatia in 1991 occurred when Yugoslavia was still in existence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can see from your CV that you graduated from your military schools in regular fashion, the military academy as well, and I assume you're familiar with the provisions that have to do with All People's Defence; is that right, Mr. 1804?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll now skip some of the general points but I'm sure you know that in the constitution of SFRY it is stated that each and every citizen who with arms takes part in resistance against the attackers is a member of the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I assume that as an educated officer yourself you're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, does that mean -- I'm asking you now, give me your example and tell me, did you consider that all those who took part in the defence of the SFRY and defence of its territorial integrity pursuant to the constitution were legal members of the armed forces, lawful ones? Would that be true?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I personally considered that those people who were in the legal units and lawfully belonged to those units were, by the same token, members of the armed forces, that is to say the police or milicija, the Territorial Defence, the JNA, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you include the volunteer units there if they are subordinated to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, if they're subordinated to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And we've already observed that if they weren't subordinated to the JNA, they were arrested, disarmed, and expelled. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, in certain cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, in view of the profession, your military profession and the rules and regulations in force at the time from your position and post, I assume you had an awareness of the fact that the character of the paramilitary formations were those formations which did not defend Yugoslavia. They were characterised as paramilitaries, and their territorial integrity -- and its territorial integrity, but did the contrary?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, there were paramilitary formations of that kind too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were formations that jeopardised the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia and acted contrary to the constitution, that is to say contrary to the law and legal provisions, and their very existence was unlawful and contrary to the provision of law; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you have experience from those days in 1991, can we conclude that, for example, the Croatian National Guard Corps, the ZNG, set up an institution that was contrary to the Yugoslav constitution; or, for example, the Patriotic League, another instance in point in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Were they paramilitary formations, in fact?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think that until those republics were recognised, these were indeed paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know since -- well, let's narrow down our focus of attention and look at Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the Patriotic League, for example, was established already in March 1991.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I don't know the exact month, whether it was March or not, but I do know that it was set up sometime in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the date exists and it is celebrated as Patriotic League Day on that particular day with them, so this is no secret.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: You're probably right although I didn't pay attention to the exact date, but I did say that I know it was sometime in 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 of your statement, say, and I'm quoting you, that: "An order was received from a higher instance that all officers and soldiers who were from the Krajina should remain in Krajina and join up the army of Krajina and that anybody else could join up with the other army." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, this superior instance that proclaimed this obligation on the -- for the Krajina citizens to join the Krajina army was quite certainly not the JNA or any kind of Yugoslav authority. It didn't have this competence and authorisation when the JNA was withdrawing from Croatia or, rather, the territory of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: We reached that -- that reached us from the superior command, which means from the corps command, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is it true that this kind of order could only have been issued by the authorities in Krajina to its own citizens and that in fact it was a component part of the general mobilisation process?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that the authorities of Krajina issued that order, but I don't know about these details as to what was going on in the Krajina. I can't say with any great precision. I'm not sufficiently aware of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know that the withdrawal of the JNA from that territory was a component part of the agreement that was reached and, generally speaking, the plan that was well known under the name of the Vance Plan when the area was placed under protection, the areas in Croatia were placed under protection?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, I do remember that there was some political negotiations, but what I remember more was that General Raseta negotiated on pulling out the JNA units, on having the JNA units pull out and that they deblocked the barracks for us and allowed us to withdraw, and I'm thinking of my particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. So up until then, the barracks in Croatia were blocked until that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The one I was in was blocked, yes, and I assume the others were too, but I'm now speaking about my own one and I say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long was your barracks blocked for? How long did the blockade of your barracks last?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, sometime after the war in Slovenia, that is to say from the summer of 1991 to the withdrawal itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you withdraw from Croatia yourself?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, that was sometime on the 10th or 11th of November, 1991, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you had spent several months under a blockade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, your particular unit at that time while it was under a blockade, did it launch any attack on its environment at all?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The unit I was in did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did -- were you fired at? Did they shoot at you?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: On several occasions. Not like they did in some other places, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not like they did in some other place, but yes, they did shoot at you, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: On several occasions. It was infantry fire on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't shoot at them at all, did you?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The order -- you had an order not to shoot?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, by our commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 12, you state the following: "When I was redeployed with my unit --" and I'm going to skip the locality you were redeployed to bearing in mind the fact that this could disclose your identity, but that's what it says in paragraph 12 of your statement, the point isn't on location itself, so: "When I was redeployed with my unit to a locality X in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were more Serb officers there than any other ethnic group." And I'm continuing with the quotation: "This, however, was mainly because the different ethnic groups had decided to join up with the armies of their own countries. For example, the Croats left to join the Croatian army, and the Slovenes went to join the Slovenian army. A part of the Muslims and the Albanians also fled the unit. Also, some political parties invited the members of their nationalities to leave the JNA or not to respond to the JNA as well as for other reasons." End of quotation. Now, my question to you is the following: Up until the war in Slovenia and Croatia, until the war broke out there and then during the war in Croatia, the JNA was multi-ethnic, as we have already observed. It included different nationalities. And then there was this change, the secession of the republics which forcibly seceded from Yugoslavia. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then that secession was followed by secession from the JNA by the members of the JNA who adopted for the secession; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Some of them left, others fled, so I don't know whether we can call that secession, but yes, they did leave our ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So what you observe, that is that it was mostly the Serb officers who remained, was not the result of any kind of act by the JNA to be rid of the members of the other ethnic groups. It was purely the fact that they had left the JNA.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to check that out with you, to verify it. I'm not claiming that you did say that. So they left the JNA. When you say that they were mostly Serb officers, that means that it wasn't only the Serb officers that stayed on, there were other ethnicities who stayed on in the JNA when you arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 14, paragraph 14 you say that amongst the officers of the JNA in Bosnia there was the fear that the Muslims and Croats in Bosnia might unilaterally try to secede from Yugoslavia and establish their own unitary state as Slovenia and Croatia had previously done. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can I conclude and take it then that the officers in the JNA, who were mostly Serbs at the time, were in favour of preserving the common state of Yugoslavia or, rather, that they wished to preserve it?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: In the majority of cases, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, since you yourself are a Serb from Bosnia-Herzegovina, did the Serb inhabitants in Bosnia-Herzegovina come out in favour of preserving Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And since Yugoslavia was a multi-ethnic state whose federal constitutional system guaranteed equal rights to all its citizens, you know full well that the Serbs -- the total Serb population in Yugoslavia was a little less than 40 per cent of the total population. This means that the Serbs strove for multi-ethnicity and equality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Most of the population, the majority of the population strove to preserve Yugoslavia, if we're talking about the Serbs in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, what about their position? Was it their position that all nationalities or ethnic groups should be equal?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: At the time we're talking about, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, since the preservation of the countries' territorial integrity was guaranteed by the constitution and since secession was banned by that same constitution, does that mean that Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Krajina and all over Yugoslavia strove to protect the constitutional order by the same token?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, I've already said they did strive to preserve Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, this fact that the Serbs strove to preserve Yugoslavia and that the JNA as a Yugoslav institution also was in favour of seeing Yugoslavia preserved, was that precisely the factor which painted an impression as to an alliance between the Serbs and the JNA, gave that impression?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. 1804. If they were essentially allies and if their goals were to respect the constitution and preserve the state and thereby stand in opposition to those toppling the state and the constitution, is it obvious that there was nothing in that that was bad, if I can put it that way, but that both acted in the moral and legal sense as dictated by the constitution and the law?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: At the beginning, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you seem to be reinvigorated for the afternoon session, but it's time to adjourn. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we are adjourning -- I see the time, yes, we are adjourning. There are administrative matters that I must deal with and I prefer to deal with in the absence of the witness, they having nothing whatsoever to do with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Witness 1804, we will adjourn for the afternoon. You are not to discuss your evidence with anybody during the adjournment, and be back tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My concern is with the following --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My concern is with following witnesses:

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we be in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 11th day of February, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
